games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W29: went, came, ran, flew, trip
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (went, came, ran, flew, trip) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Irregular Verbs: Movement (go-went, come-came, run-ran, fly-flew)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Irregular Verbs: Movement (go-went, come-came, run-ran, fly-flew).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Adventure Stories — The Magic Trip"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Adventure Stories — The Magic Trip".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (went, came, ran, flew, trip usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

teacher_contents.reading_passage: Last summer, Max went on a magic trip! He went to the beach with his family. They flew on a big airplane. "The airplane flew high in the sky!" said Max. At the beach, Max ran on the sand. He ran into the cold water. His sister came with a ball. "Come and play with me!" she said. They ran and played all day. At night, a colorful bird flew across the sky. The bird came from the green forest. Finally, they went back home. Max was tired but happy. "That was a great adventure!" he said.

listening_script.speed_note: Normal speed (130 wpm) — pause after each sentence for dictation section
listening_script.text: Last summer, Max went on a magic trip to the beach. His family flew on a big airplane. At the beach, Max ran on the sand and ran into the cold water. His sister came with a ball and they played all day. A colorful bird flew across the sky. It came from the green forest. Finally, they went back home. Max was tired but very happy.
listening_script.dictation: His sister came with a ball and they ran and played all day.

teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• Irregular verbs in past tense: go→went, come→came, run→ran, fly→flew
• These 4 verbs are the WEEK 29 target — students must produce them actively
• Key contrast: regular verbs add -ed (played, walked) / irregular verbs change form completely
• Avoid drilling as a list — keep in story context: 'Max WENT to the beach. The airplane FLEW high.'
• Spiral link: students learned was/were (W19-27) — now adding movement irregular verbs
teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Names one thing Max did at the beach (e.g., "Max ran on the sand").
Student B: Responds with what happened next using a sequence word (e.g., "Then, he ran into the water").
Goal: Use irregular verbs in past tense, chained with sequence words.

PULL-OUT TASK (S1):
— Show a picture of a beach/airplane. Ask: "What did Max do first?"
— Scaffold weak students: provide sentence frame "Max ___ to the beach. He ___ on the sand."
— Target elicitation: went / flew / ran / came

COMMUNICATIVE TASK TIP:
— If students say 'goed' or 'runned', model the correct form immediately: "We say 'went' — Max WENT to the beach."
— Stronger students: challenge them to use 3 irregular verbs in one story sentence.
teacher_contents.stem_extension:
STEM Link — Transportation & Speed (Geography/Science):
An airplane travels at ~800 km/h; a car at ~100 km/h; a person running at ~10 km/h. Ask students: 'Max flew to the beach on an airplane. If the beach is 800 km away, how long did the flight take?' (Answer: 1 hour.) Connect: 'Why do people choose airplanes for long trips?'
teacher_contents.in_class_speaking: Trip Story Chain (Pairs): Student A says the first event using 'went' (e.g., 'Last summer, I went to the beach.'). Student B continues with 'then' + a new verb (e.g., 'Then, I ran into the water.'). Continue alternating — each student must use a different irregular verb. Goal: produce a 4-event chain using went/came/ran/flew.
teacher_contents.vc_answer_key: beach, airplane, sand, cold, sister, bird, forest, home, tired, adventure

teacher_contents.reading_passage: Luna went on a trip to the mountain. First, she packed her bags. Then, her family went in a fast car. They didn't fly on an airplane. When they arrived, Luna ran up the rocky path. She ran very fast! A friendly cat came to say hello. "Hello, little cat!" said Luna. Suddenly, a big eagle flew over their heads! It flew very high in the clouds. After that, they went down the mountain safely. "The trip was amazing!" said Luna. "I want to go again next year."

listening_script.speed_note: Slightly slower (120 wpm) — this session focuses on matching task format
listening_script.text: Luna went on a trip to the mountain with her family. They went in a fast car, not an airplane. When they arrived, Luna ran up the rocky path very fast. A friendly cat came to say hello to Luna. Then, a big eagle flew over their heads. It flew very high in the clouds. After that, they went down the mountain safely. Luna said the trip was amazing.
listening_script.dictation: A big eagle flew over their heads and flew very high in the clouds.

teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• Review: went / ran / came / flew — same 4 verbs, different story context
• New usage: negative past — 'They didn't fly on an airplane.' (did + not + base form)
• Sequence words review: First / Then / When / Suddenly / After that
• 'Arrived' is regular (arrive→arrived) — contrast with irregular verbs
• Key pattern: 'Luna RAN up the path' (direction) vs 'The eagle FLEW over their heads' (direction)
teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: States one action Luna did (e.g., "Luna ran up the rocky path").
Student B: Continues with what happened next (e.g., "Then, a cat came to say hello").
Goal: 2-event chain using sequence words + irregular verbs.

PULL-OUT TASK (S2):
— Ask: 'How did Luna's family travel? Did they fly?' → elicit: 'No, they went in a car.'
— Scaffold: sentence frame 'They didn't ___. They ___.'  
— Target: distinguish 'flew' vs 'went (by car)' — two different travel verbs

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: provide verb bank (went / ran / came / flew) for Speaking Checkpoint
— Stronger students: use 'Suddenly' and 'After that' as mandatory connectors
teacher_contents.stem_extension:
STEM Link — Geography & Elevation:
Mountains are higher in elevation than beaches. The Dead Sea is 430m below sea level (lowest point on Earth); Mount Everest is 8,849m above sea level (highest). Ask: 'Luna ran UP the mountain — why does your body feel more tired going uphill?' Connect to energy, gravity, and effort. 'Eagles fly HIGH — what body features help them stay up?' (large wingspan, hollow bones).
teacher_contents.in_class_speaking: Compare & Contrast Talk (Pairs): One student describes Max's beach trip (S1), the other describes Luna's mountain trip (S2). They must use at least 3 irregular verbs each and include one similarity and one difference. Example opener: 'Max went to the beach. Luna went to the mountain. Both went on trips!' Wrap up: whole class votes — beach trip or mountain trip?
teacher_contents.vc_answer_key: mountain, car, airplane, ran, path, cat, eagle, clouds, down, amazing

teacher_contents.reading_passage: Tom went on a trip to the green forest. He wanted to see how animals move. First, a small rabbit ran out of the bushes. It ran very fast! Then, a beautiful butterfly flew in the air. It flew from flower to flower. Next, Tom went near the river. A little turtle came out of the water. It came very slowly. Finally, Tom ran back to his family. "Animals move in different ways!" he said. "Some animals fly, some animals run, and some come slowly!"

listening_script.speed_note: Normal speed (130 wpm) — Cambridge Flyers Listening Part 1 (multiple choice format)
listening_script.text: Tom went to the green forest to see how animals move. First, a small rabbit ran out of the bushes very fast. Then, a beautiful butterfly flew from flower to flower in the air. Next, Tom went near the river. A little turtle came out of the water very slowly. Finally, Tom ran back to his family. He said: 'Animals move in different ways — some fly, some run, and some come slowly!'
listening_script.dictation: A little turtle came out of the water and it came very slowly.

teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• Mastery session: all 4 irregular verbs used in one story — went / ran / flew / came
• 'Some animals fly, some run, some come slowly' — present tense for general facts vs past tense for story events
• Error prevention: butterfly 'FLEW' (not 'flied'); turtle 'CAME' (not 'comed')
• Synthesis: students can now categorize: 'ran → movement on land; flew → movement in air; came → arrival direction'
• Portfolio target: write a complete paragraph using went + ONE other irregular verb
teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Names one animal from the story and says how it moves (e.g., 'The rabbit ran fast').
Student B: Names a different animal and says how it moves (e.g., 'The butterfly flew slowly').
Goal: Use ALL FOUR irregular verbs across the pair — went / came / ran / flew.

PULL-OUT TASK (S3 — Communicative Task):
— Ask: 'Can you tell me about ALL the animals Tom saw? Use past tense.'
— Target a complete retell: 'First, a rabbit RAN... Then, a butterfly FLEW... Next, a turtle CAME... Finally, Tom RAN back.'
— Mastery check: student uses went/came/ran/flew without looking at the text.

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: 'Animal Card Retell' — give animal picture cards, student says the verb
— Stronger students: 'Add an animal' — invent one more animal that WENT into the forest
teacher_contents.stem_extension:
STEM Link — Animal Locomotion (Science):
Animals move in 3 main ways: flying (birds, insects — use wings), running (mammals, reptiles — use legs), swimming (fish, turtles — use fins/flippers). Ask: 'The butterfly FLEW and the turtle CAME out of water — which moves faster? Why?' Science extension: 'What body part helps a butterfly fly?' (wings) vs 'What body part helps a turtle move in water?' (flippers). Connect math: if a rabbit runs at 50 km/h and a turtle walks at 0.3 km/h, how many times faster is the rabbit?
teacher_contents.in_class_speaking: Animal Movement Story Circle (Group of 3): Each student picks one animal (rabbit/butterfly/turtle). Student 1: 'I am the rabbit. I ran out of the bushes.' Student 2: 'I am the butterfly. I flew from flower to flower.' Student 3: 'I am the turtle. I came out of the water slowly.' Then all three say the moral together: 'Animals move in different ways!' Repeat with new animals invented by students.
teacher_contents.vc_answer_key: forest, rabbit, bushes, butterfly, flower, river, turtle, water, slowly, different

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: The "Mirror Game" Concept
content: Problem: Students frequently confuse "is" (states) with "has" (possession), resulting in errors like "I am long hair" or "She has tall."
Solution: We use the "Mirror Game" to visually distinguish between what a person is (their state: tall, short, big, small) and what a person has (their physical features: hair, eyes, glasses).

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce physical features and the contrast between "is" and "has".
Session 2: Expand descriptions with adjectives (long, short, curly, straight).
Session 3: Consolidate full physical descriptions of self and others.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Ask the student: "Are you tall or short?" -> Student: "I am short." "Do you have big eyes?" -> Student: "I have big eyes."
S2 pull-out: Ask the student: "What kind of hair does she have?" -> Student: "She has long curly hair."
Communicative task (Section 8): Mirror Partners. Students describe their partner's appearance using "is" and "has".

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W3: tall, short, hair, eyes, long
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (tall, short, hair, eyes, long) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: "is" vs "has" (State vs Possession)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: "is" vs "has" (State vs Possession).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Identity & Environment — The Mirror Game"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Identity & Environment — The Mirror Game".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (tall, short, hair, eyes, long usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

quick_ref.Grammar Focus: Irregular Verbs: Consumption & Possession (eat-ate, drink-drank, have-had)
quick_ref.Key Pattern: "I ate a sandwich. I had some juice."
quick_ref.Vocabulary: 10 Tier 1 (production) + 0 Tier 2

quick_ref.Theme: Unit 5: Adventure Stories — The Picnic Mystery

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Problem and Solution
content: Problem: Students frequently overgeneralize the "-ed" rule for past tense, producing errors like "eated", "drinked", or "haved".

Solution: Group irregular verbs by semantic themes (Consumption & Possession) and teach them implicitly through a highly relatable context (a picnic adventure). Students internalize the correct irregular forms through repeated, meaningful exposure before explicit rule presentation.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Teacher pull-out rotation during independent time:
S1: vocabulary drill — teacher says Vietnamese/mime, student says English + makes sentence.
S2: grammar pattern practice — teacher asks "What did you eat/drink?" → student answers using key pattern.
S3: VC script rehearsal — student reads aloud, teacher gives pronunciation feedback.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: Pull-out oral tasks (teacher does these with 1–2 students while class works):
S1 pull-out: Show flashcard of base verb (e.g., "eat") → student says past form ("ate"), meaning, and 1 sentence.
S2 pull-out: Give prompt ("You were hungry. What did you do?") → student answers using the key pattern.
S3 pull-out: Student reads S3 VC script aloud → teacher recasts irregular verb mispronunciations.

Communicative task (Step 5 — 10 min — MUST have real information gap): Students work in pairs. Each student has a card with half the details of a picnic. They ask questions to complete the menu and events. Materials needed: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B per pair (Section 8). Step-by-step:
Give Student A Card A and Student B Card B. Do not show cards.
Students take turns asking the provided questions to fill in their blanks.
Students produce: A complete list of what was eaten, drunk, and had at the picnic.
ate: Mime bringing food to the mouth and chewing.
drank: Mime holding a glass and tilting head back.
had: Hold both hands flat in front of the chest, gesturing ownership.
hungry/thirsty: Rub stomach (hungry) or touch throat (thirsty).
Common errors to watch during pull-out:
Error: "I eated the apple." → Recast: "Listen: I ate the apple. What did you eat?"
Error: "He drinked juice." → Recast: "He drank juice. What did he drink?"

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The Perfect Picnic
content: Yesterday, Max and Luna went to the park. They had a big picnic under a tree. First, they played games and ran on the grass. Soon, Max was very hungry. "Let's eat!" he said. He ate a big sandwich. The sandwich was delicious! Luna was thirsty after running. She drank cold apple juice. Then, they had some fresh fruit. They ate red apples and green grapes. "This is a great picnic," said Luna. They ate, drank, and had a wonderful time. Finally, they went home, feeling very full and happy.

T / F: Luna drank cold apple juice.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Food Gives Us Energy
content: Our bodies are like machines — we need energy to move, run, and learn. We get energy from food!
• Carbohydrates (bread, rice): fast energy  • Protein (eggs, meat): build muscles  • Vitamins (fruit, veg): keep us healthy

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The Missing Sandwich
content: Luna had a small picnic in her garden. She put a delicious sandwich and a box of juice on the grass. Then, she went inside to get some fresh fruit. When Luna came back, she was very surprised. Her sandwich was gone! She was hungry, but she only had juice. She drank the juice slowly. She was still hungry. Suddenly, a little dog ran out from behind a tree. The dog licked its lips. It ate Luna's sandwich! "You bad dog!" laughed Luna. "You must be very hungry." Luna sat down and ate her fruit instead. The dog drank water from a bowl. They had a funny picnic together.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The Missing Sandwich
content: Luna had a small picnic in her garden. She put a delicious sandwich and a box of juice on the grass. Then, she went inside to get some fresh fruit. When Luna came back, she was very surprised. Her sandwich was gone! She was hungry, but she only had juice. She drank the juice slowly. She was still hungry. Suddenly, a little dog ran out from behind a tree. The dog licked its lips. It ate Luna's sandwich! "You bad dog!" laughed Luna. "You must be very hungry." Luna sat down and ate her fruit instead. The dog drank water from a bowl. They had a funny picnic together.
T / F: Luna had a picnic at the beach.
T / F: A little dog ate Luna's sandwich.
What did Luna put on the grass?
Fill-in from text: She _________ the juice slowly, but she was still _________.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ [O] Stage 3B — Inference: How do we know the dog enjoyed the sandwich? Use the text.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Why We Get Thirsty
content: [ALL] Read this: Our bodies are mostly made of water! When we run, play, or go on an adventure, we sweat. Sweating cools our body down, but we lose water. When we lose water, our brain sends a signal. This signal makes us feel thirsty. We must drink water or juice to replace the lost water. Drinking keeps our body healthy and strong!

The diagram shows: A drawing of a human body. Blue drops represent sweat leaving the body. An arrow points from the brain with a warning sign: "Thirsty!". Another arrow points to a person drinking a glass of water to refill the body.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The Perfect Picnic
content: Yesterday, Max and Luna went to the park. They had a big picnic under a tree. First, they played games and ran on the grass. Soon, Max was very hungry. "Let's eat!" he said. He ate a big sandwich. The sandwich was delicious! Luna was thirsty after running. She drank cold apple juice. Then, they had some fresh fruit. They ate red apples and green grapes. "This is a great picnic," said Luna. They ate, drank, and had a wonderful time. Finally, they went home, feeling very full and happy.
T / F: Max and Luna had a picnic at the beach.
T / F: Luna drank cold apple juice.
Fill-in from text: They _________, _________, and _________ a wonderful time.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ [O] Stage 3B — Inference: Why did they feel "very full" at the end? Use the text.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Food Gives Us Energy
content: [ALL] Read this: Our bodies are like machines. We need energy to move, run, and learn. We get energy from the food we eat and the liquids we drink. A sandwich gives us energy for playing. Fresh fruit gives us vitamins to stay healthy. Water and juice keep us hydrated when we are thirsty. A balanced picnic has different types of food!

content: [ALL] Read this: To stay healthy, we need a balanced diet. A balanced diet means eating different types of food. We need carbohydrates, like bread in a sandwich, to give us energy to run. We need vitamins from fresh fruit to keep us strong and prevent sickness. Finally, our body needs a lot of water to stay hydrated. A good picnic has all of these things!

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W30: ate, drank, had, picnic, sandwich
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (ate, drank, had, picnic, sandwich) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Irregular Verbs: Consumption & Possession (eat-ate, drink-drank, have-had)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Irregular Verbs: Consumption & Possession (eat-ate, drink-drank, have-had).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Adventure Stories — The Picnic Mystery ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Adventure Stories — The Picnic Mystery ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (ate, drank, had, picnic, sandwich usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

listening_script.text: Yesterday, Max and Luna went to the park. They had a big picnic under a tree. First, they played games and ran on the grass. Soon, Max was very hungry. "Let's eat!" he said. He ate a big sandwich. The sandwich was delicious! Luna was thirsty after running. She drank cold apple juice. Then, they had some fresh fruit. They ate red apples and green grapes. "This is a great picnic," said Luna. They ate, drank, and had a wonderful time. Finally, they went home, feeling very full and happy.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Names one thing Max or Luna ate/drank at the picnic (e.g., "Max ate a sandwich").
Student B: Adds another food or drink using had (e.g., "Luna had some juice").
Goal: Use ate / drank / had correctly in past tense without prompting.

PULL-OUT TASK (S1):
— Show a picture of a picnic basket. Ask: "What did they have for lunch?"
— Scaffold weaker students: "Max ___ a ___. Luna ___ some ___."
— Target elicitation: ate / drank / had — confirm students DON'T say "eated" or "drinked".

COMMUNICATIVE TASK TIP:
— If students say 'eated' or 'drinked', model immediately: "We say ATE and DRANK — they are irregular!"
— Stronger students: chain 3 verbs: "First, they ATE... Then, they DRANK... Finally, they HAD..."

Science: Food Gives Us Energy
[ALL] Read this: Our bodies are like machines. We need energy to move, run, and learn. We get energy from the food we eat and the liquids we drink. A sandwich gives us energy for playing. teacher_contents.reading_passage: Yesterday, Max and Luna went to the park. They had a big picnic under a tree. First, they played games and ran on the grass. Soon, Max was very hungry. "Let's eat!" he said. He ate a big sandwich. The sandwich was delicious! Luna was thirsty after running. She drank cold apple juice. They both had a wonderful time. "This is the best picnic!" said Max.
teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• eat→ate, drink→drank, have→had — three irregular verbs for consumption and possession
• Key contrast: regular verbs add -ed (played, walked) / these change completely
• Error prevention: 'eated' ✗ → ate ✓ | 'drinked' ✗ → drank ✓ | 'haved' ✗ → had ✓
• 'had' is very versatile: had a picnic / had breakfast / had a great time (possession + experience)
• Spiral link: students learned go→went (W29); this week adds three more common irregular verbs

listening_script.speed_note: Reading speed: Block B: 85wpm (Read clearly, pause between sentences, repeat each dictation sentence twice)
listening_script.text: Luna had a small picnic in her garden. She put a delicious sandwich and a box of juice on the grass. Then, she went inside to get some fresh fruit. When Luna came back, she was very surprised. Her sandwich was gone! She was hungry, but she only had juice. She drank the juice slowly. She was still hungry. Suddenly, a little dog ran out from behind a tree. The dog licked its lips. It ate Luna's sandwich! "You bad dog!" laughed Luna. "You must be very hungry." Luna sat down and ate her fruit instead. The dog drank water from a bowl. They had a funny picnic together.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Describes what Luna had in her picnic bag (e.g., "Luna had a sandwich").
Student B: Adds what she ate or drank (e.g., "She drank some juice").
Goal: Contrast had / ate / drank — three distinct irregular forms.

PULL-OUT TASK (S2):
— Ask: "What did Luna eat first? What did she drink?" → elicit full Past Simple sentences.
— Scaffold: sentence frame "First, she ate ___. Then, she drank ___. She also had ___."
— Error focus: distinguish 'had' (possess / experience) vs 'ate' (consume solid food).

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: picture cards of food/drinks — student names the verb used.
— Stronger students: retell Luna's whole picnic in 3 sentences using all three verbs.

PART 6: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION (Station C — 15 min minimum)
Science: Why We Get Thirsty
[ALL] Read this: Our bodies are mostly made of water! When we run, play, or go on an adventure, we sweat. Sweating cools our body down, but we lose water. When we lose water, our brain sends a signal. This signal makes us feel thirsty. We must drink water or juice to replace the lost water. Drinking keeps our body healthy and strong!
The diagram shows: A drawing of a human body. Blue drops represent sweat leaving the body. An arrow points from the brain with a warning sign: "Thirsty!". Another arrow points to a person drinking a glass of water to refill the body.
teacher_contents.vc_answer_key: [1] sandwich [2] had a small picnic [3] fresh fruit and juice [4] ate the delicious sandwich [5] hungry [6] ate her fresh fruit [7] thirsty [8] drank water from a bowl [9] picnic
teacher_contents.reading_passage: Luna had a small picnic in her garden. She put a delicious sandwich and a box of juice on the grass. Then, she went inside to get some fruit. When Luna came back, her sandwich was gone! She was hungry, but she only had juice. She drank the juice slowly and looked everywhere. Finally, she saw her little dog eating the sandwich. "So YOU ate my lunch!" laughed Luna.
teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• ate / drank / had — same three forms, reinforced in a new story context (Luna's garden)
• 'had' in two senses this session: had a picnic (experience) + she had juice (possession)
• Contrast: Luna DRANK juice (past, irregular) vs she DRINKS juice (present, regular)
• Error prevention tip: 'had' is also past of 'have' — students may say 'haved' in production
• Classroom drill: 'I am hungry → I ate. I am thirsty → I drank. I am happy → I had a great time.'

listening_script.text: Max wrote a story about his best holiday. "Last year, we had a holiday at the beach. First, I swam in the ocean. I was very tired and hungry! Then, my family had a big picnic on the sand. I ate a sandwich with cheese and tomatoes. It was delicious! My sister was thirsty, so she drank cold apple juice. Next, we had some sweet fruit. We ate bananas and grapes. We didn't eat any bad food. Finally, we lay on the beach and looked at the sky. We ate, drank, and rested. It was a perfect day."

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Tells one thing Max's family did on holiday (e.g., "They had a great time at the beach").
Student B: Continues with another detail (e.g., "Max ate ice cream and drank coconut juice").
Goal: Use ate / drank / had in a connected narrative — week 30 full mastery check.

PULL-OUT TASK (S3 — Communicative Task):
— Ask: "Can you describe Max's best holiday using all three verbs?"
— Target full retell: "First, they WENT to the beach. They ATE ice cream. They DRANK juice. They HAD a great time."
— Mastery check: student uses ate / drank / had fluently with sequence words.

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: "Tell me ONE thing Max ate and ONE thing he drank."
— Stronger students: invent their own holiday story using ate / drank / had / went.

STEM/CLIL Extension Notes (teacher only):

PART 6: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION (Station C — 15 min minimum)
Health: A Balanced Diet
[ALL] Read this: To stay healthy, we need a balanced diet. A balanced diet means eating different types of food. We need carbohydrates, like bread in a sandwich, to give us energy to run. We need vitamins from fresh fruit to keep us strong and prevent sickness. Finally, our body needs a lot of water to stay hydrated. A good picnic has all of these things!

Then, my family had a big picnic on the sand. I ate a sandwich with cheese. It was delicious! My sister was thirsty, so she drank coconut juice. We had such a wonderful time. 'Best holiday ever!' • Full W30 mastery: ate / drank / had all appear naturally in the beach holiday story

quick_ref.Theme: Time Detective Agency — The Forest File
quick_ref.Grammar Focus: Irregular Verbs: Perception (see-saw, hear-heard, feel-felt, smell-smelt)
quick_ref.Vocabulary: 5 Tier 1 (production) + 5 Tier 2 (reception)

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Sensory Storytelling
content: Problem: Students often write "flat" stories describing only actions (I went, I played).

Solution: This week introduces the "Perception" group of irregular verbs (saw, heard, felt, smelt). By integrating the 5 senses into storytelling, students learn to add descriptive depth to their past tense narratives.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce the 4 perception verbs using a forest adventure context. Focus on meaning and spelling.
Session 2: Practice using the verbs with descriptive adjectives (loud sound, soft leaves).
Session 3: Full production. Write a cohesive sensory recount of a past trip incorporating sequence words.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Show a flashcard (e.g., ear). Student must provide the past tense verb ("heard") and a logical sentence ("I heard a dog.").

Communicative task (Step 5 - 10 min): The Sense Detective. Student A lists three sensory clues ("I saw trees. I heard birds. I smelt flowers."). Student B must guess the location ("You went to the forest!").

F-E-L-T: FEEL → drop one E, add T

saw a shadow / a tall shadow

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The Mountain Hike
content: Last Sunday, Max and his dad went on a hike up the mountain.
First, Max saw a beautiful waterfall. The water was very clear and bright.
Then, they walked higher. Suddenly, Max heard a loud roar. He was scared!
"Don't worry," dad said. "It's just the wind in the caves."
Next, Max felt the rough rocks under his hands as he climbed.
After that, they stopped for a break. Max smelt the fresh pine trees.
Finally, they reached the top. The view was amazing!
Using all his senses made the hard climb a wonderful memory.

listening_script.speed_note: Read aloud at a normal, clear pace (85 wpm). Pause 2–3 seconds between sentences. Read the full text twice before students answer questions.
listening_script.text: Last Sunday, Leo walked in the forest. First, he saw a tall tree with green leaves. Then, he heard a loud monkey. Next, he felt the cool wind on his face. Finally, he smelt the rain coming. He ran home quickly!

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Names one thing Max saw in the forest (e.g., "Max saw tall trees and colorful birds").
Student B: Names one thing Max heard (e.g., "He heard the birds singing").
Goal: Use saw and heard correctly — two distinct perception verbs in past tense.

PULL-OUT TASK (S1):
— Show a forest picture. Ask: "If you were Max, what would you SEE? What would you HEAR?"
— Scaffold weaker students: "I SAW ___. I HEARD ___."
— Target elicitation: saw / heard — confirm students DON'T say "seed" or "heared".

COMMUNICATIVE TASK TIP:
— Model immediately if errors occur: "We say SAW (not 'seed') and HEARD (not 'heared')."
— Stronger students: chain all four verbs: "I saw ___, heard ___, felt ___, smelt ___."
teacher_contents.stem_extension:
STEM/CLIL Extension Notes (teacher only):

PART 6: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION — The 5 Senses
Our Five Senses
Read this: We use our five senses to learn about the world. We SEE with our eyes. We HEAR with our ears. We SMELL with our nose. We TASTE with our tongue. We FEEL with our skin. When you walk in a forest, you can use all your senses. You can see trees, hear birds, and smell flowers!
Inquiry task: What part of your body do you use to hear the birds? ________________________________________
teacher_contents.in_class_speaking:
IN-CLASS SPEAKING ACTIVITIES — Session 1 (teacher-led)

Activity 1 — Pair Speaking (3–5 min, pairs):
  Student A: Name a sense verb ("I heard...").
  Student B: Finish the sentence logically ("...a loud dog!").

Challenge Extension (L3 — for advanced/older students):
  [O] L3 — Fill in the blank with 3 options (8 items)
  Last week, I _______________ (see / saw / seen) a rabbit.
  I _______________ (hear / heard / hearing) a funny sound.
  She _______________ (feel / felt / feeling) the cold water.
  We _______________ (smell / smelt / smelling) the good food.
  They walked in the dark _______________ (forest / ocean / sky).
  The bird flew and I _______________ (saw / felt / smelt) it.
  I touched the blanket and it _______________ (heard / felt / saw) soft.
  The music was loud, so we _______________ (smelt / heard / saw) it clearly.
  [O] L4 — Sentence Expansion (8 items)
  Base: I saw. + Add: (a colorful bird) → ________________________________________
  Base: I heard. + Add: (the wind blowing) → ________________________________________
teacher_contents.vc_answer_key: [1] everyone [2] name [3] ten [4] forest [5] family [6] senses [7] saw [8] sky [9] heard [10] wind [11] felt [12] smelt [13] amazing
teacher_contents.reading_passage: Last weekend, Max went to the forest with his father. "I saw tall trees! I saw colorful birds! I saw a small rabbit!" said Max. He heard the birds singing. He heard the wind in the trees. It sounded magical. Max felt very happy in the forest. He smelt the fresh pine trees. "The forest smells amazing!" he said. It was the best day.
teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• see→saw, hear→heard, feel→felt, smell→smelt — four perception/sense verbs
• All four are irregular; 'smelt' is the British English irregular form (smelled is also accepted)
• Error prevention: 'seed' ✗ → saw ✓ | 'heared' ✗ → heard ✓ | 'feeled' ✗ → felt ✓
• Teaching tip: link each verb to a sense — saw (eyes), heard (ears), felt (hands/skin), smelt (nose)
• Contrast: 'saw' = past of SEE (not 'seen' — that is past participle, not Past Simple)

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

PULL-OUT TASK (S2):

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: picture sequence of Luna's walk — name the verb for each picture.
— Stronger students: tell the whole story using: heard / saw / felt / smelt (if applicable).

It was a cute rabbit. Luna walked closer to the river. She felt the cool water on her hands. It felt refreshing. Suddenly, she smelt something sweet in the air — it was wild flowers! • Session 2 reinforcement: heard / saw / felt / smelt all appear in Luna's evening walk
• Two uses of 'felt': felt the water (physical sensation) + felt peaceful (emotion) — both correct
• Pair contrast: Luna HEARD a sound (past) vs. she HEARS sounds every day (present)

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Names something Max saw on the mountain hike (e.g., "He saw a waterfall").
Student B: Names something Max heard (e.g., "He heard a loud roar").
Goal: Full W31 mastery — saw / heard / felt across a connected adventure story.

PULL-OUT TASK (S3 — Communicative Task):
— Ask: "Tell me the whole story of Max's hike using saw, heard, and felt."
— Target retell: "First, Max SAW a beautiful waterfall. Then, he HEARD a loud roar. He FELT very scared."
— Mastery check: all three verbs used correctly with sequence words.

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: provide verb prompts — point to SAW / HEARD / FELT cards.

STEM/CLIL Extension Notes (teacher only):

PART 6: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION — Animal Senses
Super Senses
Read this: Animals have super senses! An owl can SEE in the dark. A dog can HEAR sounds very far away. A bear can SMELL food hidden under the snow. Animals use their amazing senses to survive in the forest and the mountains.
Write 2 sentences applying the CLIL concept:
An owl can ________________________________________
A dog can ________________________________________
teacher_contents.in_class_speaking: Forest Senses Carousel (Groups of 4): Each student picks a different sense verb (saw/heard/felt/smelt). Teacher shows a forest picture. Each student says one sentence from their character's point of view using their verb. E.g., Saw: 'Max saw a tall waterfall.' Heard: 'Max heard a loud roar.' Felt: 'Max felt the cold air.' Smelt: 'Max smelt the pine trees.' Then rotate — each student uses a different verb. Goal: all four irregular forms produced by every student.

teacher_contents.reading_passage: Last Sunday, Max and his dad went on a hike up the mountain. First, Max saw a beautiful waterfall. The water was very clear and bright. Then, they walked higher. Suddenly, Max heard a loud roar. He was scared! "Don't worry," dad said. "It's just the wind." Next, Max felt the cold mountain air. He smelt fresh pine trees. Finally, he felt very brave and proud.
teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• Full W31 mastery: saw / heard / felt / smelt all in one mountain adventure story
• 'felt' used twice again: felt the cold air (sensation) + felt brave (emotion) — reinforces dual use
• Error focus this session: 'he seed the waterfall' is a very common student error → always 'SAW'
• Spiral: W29 (went) + W30 (ate, drank, had) + W31 (saw, heard, felt, smelt) = 8 irregular verbs total
• Communicative task: students retell the hike using all 4 sense verbs — mastery checkpoint

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Problem and Solution
content: Problem: Students tend to mix up the verbs "do" and "make", and often fail to produce their irregular past tense forms ("did" and "made") accurately.

Solution: Group "task" verbs (do, make, have, take) together within a highly relatable context (daily chores and routines). By anchoring these verbs to specific, frequent collocations (did homework, made the bed, took a shower), students memorize the verb phrases as single cognitive chunks.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Teacher pull-out rotation during independent time:
S1: vocabulary drill — teacher says Vietnamese/mime, student says English + makes sentence.
S2: grammar pattern practice — teacher asks "What did you do yesterday?" → student answers using past task verbs.
S3: VC script rehearsal — student reads aloud, teacher provides pronunciation feedback.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: Pull-out oral tasks (teacher does these with 1–2 students while class works):
S1 pull-out: Show flashcard of base verb ("make") → student says past form ("made"), meaning, and 1 sentence ("I made my bed").
S2 pull-out: Prompt a scenario ("Your room was a mess"). Student answers using key verbs ("I did my chores and made my bed").
S3 pull-out: Assess VC script fluency. Check for overgeneralization errors like "maked" or "taked".

Communicative task (Step 5 — 10 min — MUST have real information gap): Students work in pairs to discover a character's busy schedule. Materials needed: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B per pair (Section 8). Step-by-step:
Give Card A to Student A, Card B to Student B. Ensure they hide their cards.
Students ask provided questions to complete the missing tasks.
Students produce: A fully ordered daily schedule using sequence words and task verbs.
did: Cross arms and nod firmly (task completed).
made: Mime shaping something with hands.
took (a photo/shower): Mime clicking a camera OR scrubbing hair under water.
mess: Wiggle fingers randomly in the air to show chaos.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Health: Why We Need a Routine
content: Health: Why We Need a Routine

[ALL] Read this: A routine is what we do every day in the same order. Having a routine is very healthy! When we wake up and have a healthy breakfast, our brain gets energy. When we take a shower, we wash away sweat and invisible germs. This keeps our skin clean. Doing chores teaches us responsibility. Doing homework exercises our brain. A good routine helps us grow strong and smart!

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The Weekend Mess
content: On Saturday morning, Max had a big breakfast. Then, he played with all his toys. He built a castle and drew pictures. Soon, his bedroom was a giant mess! "Max, look at this mess!" Mom said. "Did you make your bed?" "No, I didn't," Max said. "I am sorry." Max started to do his chores. First, he made his bed neatly. Then, he put the toys away. He did his math homework at his desk. When the room was clean, Mom took a photo of it. "Great job!" she smiled. Max took a shower because he was sweaty and tired. He felt proud of his clean room.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: How Cameras Work
content: [ALL] Read this: When we take a photo, we capture light! A camera has a hole called a lens. Light bounces off an object (like a tree) and enters the lens. Inside the camera, there is a special screen. The screen saves the light as an image. This is how we remember a moment. Our eyes work the same way! Light enters our eyes so we can see the world.
The diagram shows: Light hitting a green tree. An arrow shows the light traveling from the tree into a camera lens. Inside the camera, a small picture of the tree appears on a screen.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Social Studies: Teamwork and Chores
content: [ALL] Read this: A house needs a lot of work to stay clean. If one person does all the chores, it takes a long time. They feel tired. This is why teamwork is important! When a family works together, tasks are easier. One person makes the bed. Another person does the dishes. Another person takes out the trash. The mess disappears quickly. Teamwork saves time and makes everyone happy!

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: How Cameras Work
content: [ALL] Read this: When we take a photo, we capture light! A camera has a hole called a lens. Light bounces off an object (like a tree) and enters the lens. Inside the camera, there is a special screen. The screen saves the light as an image. This is how we remember a moment. Our eyes work the same way! Light enters our eyes so we can see the world.
The diagram shows: Light hitting a green tree. An arrow shows the light traveling from the tree into a camera lens. Inside the camera, a small picture of the tree appears on a screen.

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W32: did, made, had, took, homework
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (did, made, had, took, homework) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Irregular Verbs: Tasks (do-did, make-made, have-had, take-took)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Irregular Verbs: Tasks (do-did, make-made, have-had, take-took).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Adventure Stories — The Chore File"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Adventure Stories — The Chore File".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (did, made, had, took, homework usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Problem and Solution
content: Problem: Students frequently over-apply the "-ed" rule to irregular verbs related to accidents or mistakes, resulting in errors like "breaked", "falled", "losed", or "finded".

Solution: Group these specific verbs under an "Accidents and Mistakes" theme. By attaching these irregular past tense forms to strong emotional contexts (surprise, regret, relief) and a "bad day" narrative, students form stronger cognitive anchors for the correct spellings and pronunciations.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Teacher pull-out rotation during independent time:
S1: vocabulary drill — teacher says Vietnamese/mime, student says English + makes sentence.
S2: grammar pattern practice — teacher asks "What went wrong?" → student answers using irregular accident verbs.
S3: VC script rehearsal — student reads aloud, teacher provides pronunciation feedback.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: Pull-out oral tasks (teacher does these with 1–2 students while class works):
S1 pull-out: Show flashcard of base verb ("lose") → student says past form ("lost"), meaning, and 1 sentence ("I lost my pencil").
S2 pull-out: Give a scenario ("You dropped a glass"). Student responds using key verbs ("I broke the glass. It was an accident!").
S3 pull-out: Assess VC script fluency. Check for overgeneralization errors.

Communicative task (Step 5 — 10 min — MUST have real information gap): Students work in pairs. Each has a card showing different missing items and accidents. They ask questions to solve the mystery of the bad day. Materials needed: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B per pair (Section 8). Step-by-step:
Give Card A to Student A, Card B to Student B. Ensure they hide their cards.
Students ask the provided questions to complete the missing events.
Students produce: A fully solved sequence of events.
broke: Mime snapping a stick in half over the knee.
lost: Shrug shoulders and look around confused.
found: Point index finger up and smile brightly (like an idea bulb).
clumsy: Pretend to trip and stumble.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  Tom's Bad Day
content: Poor Tom! Yesterday was a bad day! First, he fell out of bed. Ouch! Then, he broke his glasses. "Oh no! I broke them!" he said. His mom was not angry. "Accidents happen," she said. At school, Tom lost his pencil case. "I lost it! Where is it?" he looked everywhere. A friend found it under the desk. "I found your pencil case!" she said. "Thank you!" said Tom. At home, Tom broke a plate. "I am so sorry, Mom! I am clumsy today!" "Be more careful," said Mom. "But don't worry. We can fix it." Finally, Tom found his lost homework. It fell behind the bookshelf! "What a day!" said Tom.
T / F: Tom had a very good day yesterday.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Gravity and Falling
content: Gravity is the invisible force that pulls all objects DOWN towards the Earth. It never stops!
• Isaac Newton saw an apple FALL from a tree and discovered gravity (~1666)
• Gravity pulls all objects at the same speed: 9.8 m/s² (when there is no air resistance)
1. Why do things fall to the ground and not float into the sky?
2. True or False: A heavy book and a light pen fall at different speeds in space (no air).
3. Tom dropped a ball. It fell to the ground. Which force caused this?
4. Write 1 sentence using 'fell': The apple fell __________________ because of gravity.
5. Write 1 sentence using 'broke': The plate broke __________________ when it hit the ground.
Challenge: What would the world be like without gravity? Write 1 fun sentence.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  Luna's Clumsy Day
content: On Saturday, Luna wanted to help her dad. Dad was building a birdhouse in the garden. "Can I help?" asked Luna. "Yes, but be careful," Dad said. Luna carried a box of nails. Suddenly, she tripped over a rock and fell! The box broke, and the nails fell in the grass. "Oh no! It was an accident. I am clumsy today," Luna cried. "Are you okay?" Dad asked. "Don't cry. We can fix it." Luna was sorry for the mistake. She looked in the green grass. After ten minutes, she found all the lost nails! Dad smiled and they built the birdhouse together. "Next time, I will be more careful," Luna promised.

content: Poor Tom! Yesterday was a bad day! First, he fell out of bed. Ouch! Then, he broke his glasses. "Oh no! I broke them!" he said. His mom was not angry. "Accidents happen," she said. At school, Tom lost his pencil case. "I lost it! Where is it?" he looked everywhere. A friend found it under the desk. "I found your pencil case!" she said. "Thank you!" said Tom. At home, Tom broke a plate. "I am so sorry, Mom! I am clumsy today!" "Be more careful," said Mom. "But don't worry. We can fix it." Finally, Tom found his lost homework. It fell behind the bookshelf! "What a day!" said Tom.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Gravity and Falling
content: [ALL] Read this: Why do things fall? When you drop a plate, it falls to the ground. When you jump, you come back down. This happens because of a force called GRAVITY. Gravity is an invisible pull. The Earth is very big, so it has a strong gravity. It pulls everything toward its center. If there was no gravity, we would float into the sky! Gravity keeps us safe, but it also means things break when they fall!

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Materials and Breaking
content: [ALL] Read this: Why do some things break when they fall, but other things do not? It depends on the MATERIAL! Glass and ceramics are rigid (hard) but brittle. This means they break or shatter easily when they hit a hard floor. Rubber and plastic are flexible or bouncy. They can bend and absorb the shock of falling. If you are clumsy, it is better to use a plastic cup. It is safer!

content: Poor Tom! Yesterday was a bad day! First, he fell out of bed. Ouch! Then, he broke his glasses. "Oh no! I broke them!" he said. His mom was not angry. "Accidents happen," she said. At school, Tom lost his pencil case. "I lost it! Where is it?" he looked everywhere. A friend found it under the desk. "I found your pencil case!" she said. "Thank you!" said Tom. At home, Tom broke a plate. "I am so sorry, Mom! I am clumsy today!" "Be more careful," said Mom. "But don't worry. We can fix it." Finally, Tom found his lost homework. It fell behind the bookshelf! "What a day!" said Tom.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Materials and Breaking
content: [ALL] Read this: Why do some things break when they fall, but other things do not? It depends on the MATERIAL! Glass and ceramics are rigid (hard) but brittle. This means they break or shatter easily when they hit a hard floor. Rubber and plastic are flexible or bouncy. They can bend and absorb the shock of falling. If you are clumsy, it is better to use a plastic cup. It is safer!
The diagram shows: Two cups falling. On the left, a glass cup hits the ground and breaks into many sharp pieces. On the right, a plastic cup hits the ground and bounces safely.

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W33: broke, fell, lost, found, mistake
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (broke, fell, lost, found, mistake) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Irregular Verbs: Accidents (break-broke, fall-fell, lose-lost, find-found)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Irregular Verbs: Accidents (break-broke, fall-fell, lose-lost, find-found).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Adventure Stories — The Accident File ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Adventure Stories — The Accident File ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (broke, fell, lost, found, mistake usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

listening_script.text: Poor Tom! Yesterday was a bad day! First, he fell out of bed. Ouch! Then, he broke his glasses. "Oh no! I broke them!" he said. His mom was not angry. "Accidents happen," she said. At school, Tom lost his pencil case. "I lost it! Where is it?" he looked everywhere. A friend found it under the desk. "I found your pencil case!" she said. "Thank you!" said Tom. At home, Tom broke a plate. "I am so sorry, Mom! I am clumsy today!" "Be more careful," said Mom. "But don't worry. We can fix it." Finally, Tom found his lost homework. It fell behind the bookshelf! "What a day!" said Tom.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Names one accident from Tom's bad day (e.g., "Tom fell out of bed").
Student B: Names another (e.g., "He broke his glasses").
Goal: Use fell / broke correctly — two distinct accident verbs in past tense.

PULL-OUT TASK (S1):
— Show a 'bad day' illustration. Ask: "What happened to Tom first? What happened next?"
— Scaffold weaker students: "First, Tom ___ out of bed. Then, he ___ his glasses."
— Target elicitation: fell / broke — confirm students DON'T say 'falled' or 'breaked'.

COMMUNICATIVE TASK TIP:
— Model immediately: "We say FELL (not 'falled') and BROKE (not 'breaked')."
— Stronger students: add lost / found: "He also LOST his bag but FOUND it under the table."

Science: Gravity and Falling
[ALL] Read this: Why do things fall? When you drop a plate, it falls to the ground. When you jump, you come back down. This happens because of a force called GRAVITY. Gravity is an invisible pull. The Earth is very big, so it has a strong gravity. It pulls everything toward its center. If there was no gravity, we would float into the sky! Gravity keeps us safe, but it also means things break when they fall!

teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• break→broke, fall→fell, lose→lost, find→found — four accident and discovery verbs
• Paired opposites: lose ↔ find (two sides of the same event)
• Error prevention: 'breaked' ✗ → broke ✓ | 'falled' ✗ → fell ✓ | 'losed' ✗ → lost ✓ | 'founded' ✗ → found ✓
• Phonics note: 'found' rhymes with 'round/sound'; 'fell' rhymes with 'bell/well' — helps memory
• Narrative tip: these verbs often appear in sequence — 'He fell, then he broke, then he lost...'

listening_script.text: On Saturday, Luna wanted to help her dad. Dad was building a birdhouse in the garden. "Can I help?" asked Luna. "Yes, but be careful," Dad said. Luna carried a box of nails. Suddenly, she tripped over a rock and fell! The box broke, and the nails fell in the grass. "Oh no! It was an accident. I am clumsy today," Luna cried. "Are you okay?" Dad asked. "Don't cry. We can fix it." Luna was sorry for the mistake. She looked in the green grass. After ten minutes, she found all the lost nails! Dad smiled and they built the birdhouse together. "Next time, I will be more careful," Luna promised.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Describes what Luna was trying to do (e.g., "Luna wanted to help her dad build a birdhouse").
Student B: Names what went wrong (e.g., "She fell and broke a piece").
Goal: Use fell / broke / lost / found in a cause-and-effect sentence.

PULL-OUT TASK (S2):
— Ask: "What did Luna do wrong? What happened because of the accident?"
— Scaffold: "Luna was helping when she ___ and ___. Then, she ___."
— Error focus: 'lost' vs 'found' — pair them: "She LOST the hammer but FOUND it later."

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: timeline cards — put Luna's accident story in order.
— Stronger students: retell using all four verbs: "Luna fell, broke, lost, and finally found..."

Science: Materials and Breaking
[ALL] Read this: Why do some things break when they fall, but other things do not? It depends on the MATERIAL! Glass and ceramics are rigid (hard) but brittle. This means they break or shatter easily when they hit a hard floor. Rubber and plastic are flexible or bouncy. They can bend and absorb the shock of falling. If you are clumsy, it is better to use a plastic cup. It is safer!

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Problem and Solution
content: Problem: Students struggle to use multiple irregular verbs seamlessly in a continuous narrative, often switching back to the present tense or defaulting to regular "-ed" endings when cognitive load increases.

Solution: Guide students through retelling a classic fable ("The Lion and the Mouse") across three sessions. By anchoring the verbs to the Beginning, Middle, and End of a highly familiar and emotional story, students practice mixed irregular verbs in a natural, cohesive context.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Teacher pull-out rotation during independent time:
S1: vocabulary drill — teacher says Vietnamese/mime, student says English + makes sentence.
S2: grammar pattern practice — teacher asks "What did the lion/mouse do?" → student answers using irregular verbs.
S3: VC script rehearsal — student reads aloud, teacher provides pronunciation feedback.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: Pull-out oral tasks (teacher does these with 1–2 students while class works):
S1 pull-out: Show flashcard of base verb ("catch") → student says past form ("caught"), meaning, and 1 sentence.
S2 pull-out: Give a story prompt ("The lion was in the net"). Student responds using key verbs ("He felt scared and roared loudly").
S3 pull-out: Assess VC script fluency. Check for overgeneralization errors like "catched" or "waked".

Communicative task (Step 5 — 10 min — MUST have real information gap): Students work in pairs to piece together missing parts of the fable. Materials needed: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B per pair (Section 8). Step-by-step:
Give Card A to Student A, Card B to Student B. Ensure they hide their cards.
Students ask the provided questions to complete the missing story events.
Students produce: A fully ordered sequence of the fable's events.
woke: Close eyes, then snap them open and stretch.
caught: Clap hands together quickly like a trap shutting.
lion: Make claw hands and pretend to roar.
net: Cross fingers together like a grid.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The Lion and the Mouse
content: Once upon a time, there was a big lion and a tiny mouse. One day, the mouse ran across the lion's paw. The lion woke up. He was angry! "I will eat you!" said the lion. "Please don't!" said the mouse. "One day, I will help you!" The lion laughed. But he let the mouse go. A few days later, hunters came to the forest. They caught the lion in a net! The lion roared loudly. He felt scared. The tiny mouse heard the lion. "I will help you!" said the mouse. The mouse chewed the net. The lion was free! "Thank you, little friend!" said the lion. "You helped me!" The lion learned: Even small friends can help in big ways.
T / F: The mouse ate the lion.
T / F: The lion learned a good lesson.
What did the mouse do first?
What happened to the lion in the forest?

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Big and Small Animals
content: Science: Big Animals and Small Animals
In nature, animals come in all sizes — and each size has advantages!

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Symbiosis (Helping Each Other)
content: Science: Symbiosis — When Animals Help Each Other
Symbiosis means two different animals living together and BOTH benefiting. It is a win-win relationship!
• Crocodile + bird (plover): bird eats food from croc teeth → croc gets clean teeth, bird gets food
• Clownfish + sea anemone: fish hides in anemone → anemone gets protection, fish gets shelter
1. In the lion and mouse story, who helped who? Was it symbiosis?
2. True or False: In symbiosis, only ONE animal benefits.

4. Write 1 sentence using 'said': The lion said __________________ to the mouse.
5. Write 1 sentence using 'won': In the end, __________________ won because __________________.
Challenge: Can you think of a real-life example of HUMAN symbiosis (people helping each other)? Write 1 sentence.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Big and Small Animals
content: [ALL] Read this: In nature, animals come in all sizes. The lion is a large mammal. It has sharp teeth and strong muscles. It is a powerful predator. The mouse is a tiny mammal. parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Science: Symbiosis (Helping Each Other)
content: [ALL] Read this: In the wild, different animals sometimes help each other. This is a special relationship called "symbiosis" or mutualism. For example, a small bird cleans the teeth of a big crocodile! The bird gets yummy food, and the crocodile gets clean teeth without going to the dentist. In our story, the mouse and the lion helped each other. When two different animals work together, they both survive and win!
The diagram shows: A big green crocodile with its mouth wide open. A tiny white bird is standing inside the mouth, eating bugs from the crocodile's teeth. Both animals look happy.
🔍 YouTube for teacher: Search "symbiosis for kids animal friends" to find a short video.

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W34: ran, woke, said, came, caught
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (ran, woke, said, came, caught) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Mixed irregular verbs in storytelling
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Mixed irregular verbs in storytelling.
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Adventure Stories — The Classic Story File"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Adventure Stories — The Classic Story File".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (ran, woke, said, came, caught usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

chanting.script:
[W34.CHANT.1] Bright, colorful, 2D flat cartoon style, 4-second looping clip, clean white background, no real people: Animated storybook opening + bold text pulses on screen in sync + Audio: "Story! Story! Let's read a story!" (120bpm, energetic child voice).
[W34.CHANT.2] Bright, colorful, 2D flat cartoon style, 7-second looping clip, clean white background, no real people: Animated shoes running quickly + bold text pulses progressively + Audio: "Ran! Ran fast! I ran fast!" (120bpm, energetic child voice).
[W34.CHANT.3] Bright, colorful, 2D flat cartoon style, 7-second looping clip, clean white background, no real people: Animated eyes popping open + bold text pulses progressively + Audio: "Woke! Woke up! I woke up early!" (120bpm, energetic child voice).
[W34.CHANT.4] Bright, colorful, 2D flat cartoon style, 7-second looping clip, clean white background, no real people: Animated speech bubble popping out + bold text pulses progressively + Audio: "Said! Said hello! He said hello!" (120bpm, energetic child voice).
[W34.CHANT.5] Bright, colorful, 2D flat cartoon style, 7-second looping clip, clean white background, no real people: Animated person walking closer + bold text pulses progressively + Audio: "Came! Came back! She came back!" (120bpm, energetic child voice).
[W34.CHANT.6] Bright, colorful, 2D flat cartoon style, 7-second looping clip, clean white background, no real people: Animated hands grabbing a net + bold text pulses progressively + Audio: "Caught! Caught a mouse! I caught a mouse!" (120bpm, energetic child voice).
[W34.CHANT.7] Bright, colorful, 2D flat cartoon style, 4-second looping clip, clean white background, no real people: Split screen showing eyes opening and shoes running + bold text pulses on screen in sync + Audio: "Woke up early! Ran very fast!" (120bpm, energetic child voice).
[W34.CHANT.8] Bright, colorful, 2D flat cartoon style, 4-second looping clip, clean white background, no real people: Split screen showing walking closer and grabbing a net + bold text pulses on screen in sync + Audio: "She came back! I caught a mouse!" (120bpm, energetic child voice).
[W34.CHANT.9] Bright, colorful, 2D flat cartoon style, 6-second clip, clean white background, no real people: Rapid flashes of running, waking up, speaking, and catching + bold text pulses rapidly + Audio: "Ran! Woke! Said! Came! Caught!" (120bpm, energetic child voice).

listening_script.text: Once upon a time, there was a big lion and a tiny mouse. One day, the mouse ran across the lion's paw. The lion woke up. He was angry! "I will eat you!" said the lion. "Please don't!" said the mouse. "One day, I will help you!" The lion laughed. But he let the mouse go. A few days later, hunters came to the forest. They caught the lion in a net! The lion roared loudly. He felt scared. The tiny mouse heard the lion. "I will help you!" said the mouse. The mouse chewed the net. The lion was free! "Thank you, little friend!" said the lion. "You helped me!" The lion learned: Even small friends can help in big ways.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Describes what the mouse did (e.g., "The tiny mouse ran across the lion's paw").
Student B: Describes what the lion did (e.g., "The lion caught the mouse").
Goal: Use ran / caught / heard in a fable retell — mixed irregular verbs.

PULL-OUT TASK (S1):
— Show lion and mouse pictures. Ask: "What happened first? What did the lion say?"
— Scaffold weaker students: "The mouse ___ across the paw. The lion ___ it."
— Target elicitation: ran / caught — confirm students don't say 'runned' or 'catched'.

COMMUNICATIVE TASK TIP:
— Model: "We say RAN (not 'runned') and CAUGHT (not 'catched')."
— Stronger students: add moral reasoning — "Why did the lion let the mouse go free?"

It does not have big muscles, but it is very fast and can hide in small spaces. Big animals are strong, but small animals are clever and quick. Every animal has special skills to survive in the wild!

listening_script.text: Detective Luna is reading the middle of the fable. A few days after meeting the mouse, the lion was walking in the forest. Suddenly, hunters came to the forest. They caught the big lion in a strong net! The lion could not escape. He was trapped. He roared very loudly because he was angry. Then, he felt scared. Who could help him? Far away, the tiny mouse heard the loud roar. The mouse knew his friend was in trouble. The mouse ran fast to find the lion. "Do not worry!" said the mouse. "I am small, but I can help!" The lion was surprised to see the tiny mouse again.

PART 6: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION (Station C — 15 min minimum)
Science: How Nets Work
[ALL] Read this: A net is a very useful tool! It is made of ropes or strong threads. The ropes are tied together in knots to make a pattern with holes. Nets are strong because the weight or pulling force is shared across many ropes. Hunters use nets to catch heavy animals. Fishermen use nets to catch many fish. But there is a weakness: if one rope is chewed or cut, the whole net can break!
The diagram shows: A drawing of a net made of criss-crossing ropes. A pair of scissors is cutting one small rope, making a big hole in the net.

listening_script.text: Max is presenting the end of the fable to the class. "The mouse saw the lion caught in the net. The mouse said, 'I will help you!' The mouse used his sharp teeth. He chewed the net. He chewed and chewed until the hole was big. Finally, the lion was free! The lion felt very happy. He looked at the tiny mouse. 'Thank you, little friend!' said the lion. teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student B: Completes the story (e.g., "The mouse chewed the net and the lion ran free").
Goal: W34 mastery — full fable retell using: ran / saw / heard / came / fell / found.

PULL-OUT TASK (S3 — Communicative Task):
— Ask: "Can you retell the whole Lion and Mouse story from beginning to end?"
— Target: "Once, a mouse RAN across a lion. The lion CAUGHT it. Later, the lion FELL into a net. The mouse CAME and FOUND the lion. The mouse CHEWED the net. The lion RAN free."
— Mastery check: student retells all three parts without looking at the text.

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: use three-part prompt cards (beginning / middle / end).
— Stronger students: connect the moral to real life — "When did someone help you like the mouse helped the lion?"

STEM/CLIL Extension Notes (teacher only):

PART 6: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION (Station C — 15 min minimum)
Science: Symbiosis (Helping Each Other)
[ALL] Read this: In the wild, different animals sometimes help each other. This is a special relationship called "symbiosis" or mutualism. For example, a small bird cleans the teeth of a big crocodile! The bird gets yummy food, and the crocodile gets clean teeth without going to the dentist. In our story, the mouse and the lion helped each other. When two different animals work together, they both survive and win!
The diagram shows: A big green crocodile with its mouth wide open. A tiny white bird is standing inside the mouth, eating bugs from the crocodile's teeth. Both animals look happy.

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Storytelling with Irregular Verbs
content: Problem: Students often apply the regular "-ed" rule to irregular verbs.

Solution: This week anchors 5 high-frequency irregular verbs (went, saw, felt, made, gave) to a highly personal, emotional context: "My Best Day Ever." By connecting the irregular form to a vivid memory, students memorize the chunk rather than analyzing the rule.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce the 5 irregular verbs through a recount of a beach trip. Focus on meaning and form recognition.
Session 2: Practice the verbs with sequence words (First, Then) to build narrative flow.
Session 3: Full production. Students write and present their own "Best Day" story using the target verbs without scaffolding.

methodology.title: 2.3 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Hand the student a base verb card (go). The student must physically step forward and say the past form (went) in a full sentence.
Communicative task (Step 5 - 10 min): Information Gap: The Mystery Trip. Student A has the morning events. Student B has the afternoon events. They ask questions to complete the itinerary.

parts.title: PART 6: STEM/CLIL — Floating and Sinking
content: Science: Why Things Float and Sink
Objects float when they are LESS DENSE than water. They sink when they are MORE DENSE than water!
• Density = how much 'stuff' is packed into a space  • Cork floats  • Iron sinks
• A steel ship FLOATS because it is shaped to trap air — air is very light!
1. A paper boat FLOATS. A metal coin SINKS. What is the difference?
