games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W35: went, saw, felt, made, gave
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (went, saw, felt, made, gave) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Past Simple (Irregular Verbs: went, saw, felt, made, gave)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Past Simple (Irregular Verbs: went, saw, felt, made, gave).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Adventure Stories — My Best Day ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Adventure Stories — My Best Day ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (went, saw, felt, made, gave usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

listening_script.speed_note: Read aloud at a normal, clear pace (85 wpm). Pause 2–3 seconds between sentences. Read the full text twice before students answer questions.
listening_script.text: Last Sunday, Leo went to the beach with his friends. First, he saw a big ship on the water. Then, he made a large sandcastle. He felt very proud. Finally, his friend gave him a cool shell. It was a great trip.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Names one thing Max did at the beach on his best day (e.g., "Max went to the beach and made a sandcastle").
Student B: Adds what Max felt or what his mom gave (e.g., "His mom gave him a shell. He felt very happy").
Goal: Use went / made / felt / gave correctly — W35 irregular verbs in a personal story.

PULL-OUT TASK (S1):
— Show a beach picture. Ask: "What did Max do? What did his mom give him?"
— Scaffold weaker students: "Max WENT to ___. He MADE ___. He FELT ___."
— Target elicitation: went / made / felt / gave — confirm no 'maked', 'gived', or 'feeled'.

COMMUNICATIVE TASK TIP:
— Model immediately: "We say MADE (not 'maked'), GAVE (not 'gived'), FELT (not 'feeled')."
— Stronger students: chain all 5 verbs: "Max WENT to the beach. He SAW shells. He MADE a castle. His mom GAVE him a bag. He FELT proud."
teacher_contents.stem_extension:
STEM/CLIL Extension Notes (teacher only):

PART 6: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION — Ocean Ecosystems Crabs on the Beach Read this: A crab is a small ocean animal. It lives on the beach and in the water. A crab has a hard shell to protect its body. It has two big claws to catch food. Crabs walk sideways on the sand! They eat tiny plants and animals in the ocean.
The diagram shows: A crab with a hard round shell in the middle, eight legs for walking, and two sharp claws at the front.
Inquiry task: Why does a crab need a hard shell? ________________________________________
🔍 YouTube: "How crabs walk and eat for kids"

teacher_contents.reading_passage: Last summer, Max went to the beach with his mom. First, he saw beautiful white shells on the sand. He picked them up and made a big sandcastle near the water. "Look, Mom!" he said. His mom gave him a big bag for all the shells. Max felt very happy and proud. At sunset, he was tired but he smiled. "Today was my best day ever," Max said.
teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• went (W29), saw (W31), felt (W31), made (W32), gave — five key irregular verbs; gave is the new focus
• give→gave is highly irregular and very common — 'gived' ✗ is a very frequent student error
• Contrast: gave (past) vs gives (present 3rd person) — 'Mom GIVES him things. Today, she GAVE him a bag.'
• 'felt' returns: Max felt happy — reinforces W31 feel→felt in a new personal context
• Tip: 'gave' appears in many high-frequency phrases: gave me a hug / gave me a gift / gave me advice

listening_script.text: Last Friday, Anna went to the mountains. First, she saw a large forest. Then, she made a small fire with her dad. She felt very warm. Finally, her dad gave her some hot soup. It was a wonderful evening.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Describes what Luna saw at the zoo (e.g., "Luna saw a tall giraffe").
Student B: Adds what the zookeeper gave them and how Luna felt (e.g., "The zookeeper gave them food. She felt excited").
Goal: saw / gave / felt / went — perception + emotion + action verbs.

PULL-OUT TASK (S2):
— Ask: "What was the best thing Luna saw? How did she feel?"
— Scaffold: "First, she WENT to the zoo. She SAW ___. A zookeeper GAVE them ___. She FELT ___."
— Error focus: 'gave' — confirm students don't say 'gived' or 'given' (given = past participle, not Past Simple).

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: picture of a zoo — name one animal Luna SAW and one emotion she FELT.
— Stronger students: full retell using all 5 verbs: went / saw / felt / made / gave.

PART 6: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION — Animal Diets What Do Giraffes Eat? Read this: A giraffe is a very tall animal. It has a long neck and long legs. Giraffes eat leaves from high trees. They do not eat meat. An animal that only eats plants is called a herbivore. A giraffe uses its long, dark tongue to pull leaves off the branches.
The diagram shows: A tall yellow giraffe with brown spots using its long neck to reach green leaves on a high tree branch.
Inquiry task: Why do giraffes need a long neck? ________________________________________ 🔍 YouTube: "Giraffe eating leaves for kids"
teacher_contents.in_class_speaking: Best Day Retell (Pairs): Student A describes Luna's zoo day in 3 sentences using saw / felt / gave. Student B describes Max's beach day in 3 sentences using went / made / felt. Then swap. Goal: both students produce all five W35 verbs. Extension — stronger students: Tell your own best day using all 5 verbs.

teacher_contents.reading_passage: Last Saturday, Luna went to the zoo with her class. First, she saw a tall, beautiful giraffe. "Wow!" she said. Then, a kind zookeeper gave Luna and her classmates some special animal food to hold. Luna felt very excited! She also saw funny monkeys jumping everywhere. She felt so happy that she laughed and laughed. She made a drawing in her notebook to remember the day.
teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• Session 2: went / saw / felt / made / gave — same five verbs, zoo adventure context
• 'gave' used naturally: the zookeeper GAVE them food — reinforces the form in a new subject
• Two uses of 'felt': felt excited (first reaction) + felt happy (continued emotion) — shows flexibility
• Question drill: 'What did the zookeeper give Luna?' → 'She gave her animal food.'
• Common error: students say 'the zookeeper gived' — model and correct immediately

listening_script.text: Last Saturday, Tom went to the library. First, he saw many amazing books. Then, he read a story and felt very excited. Next, he made a special bookmark. Finally, the librarian gave him a sticker for reading well.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Describes what Max and his dad made at the park (e.g., "Max and his dad made a kite").
Student B: Continues with what happened later (e.g., "His dad gave him lunch. Max felt completely relaxed").
Goal: W35 final mastery — went / saw / felt / made / gave in a complete best-day narrative.

PULL-OUT TASK (S3 — Communicative Task):
— Ask: "Tell me about YOUR best day. Use went, saw, felt, made, and gave."
— Target personal response: "I WENT to ___. I SAW ___. We MADE ___. Someone GAVE me ___. I FELT ___."
— Mastery check: all 5 verbs correct, personal context used.

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: "Tell me just ONE thing you made and ONE thing someone gave you."

The water pushes up against the flat bottom of the boat. If you put heavy stones in the paper boat, it will sink. The paper will also get wet and tear after a long time.

Together they build a 'Best Day' story. Then rotate so each student uses a different verb. Goal: every student produces all five W35 irregular verbs by the end.

teacher_contents.reading_passage: On Sunday, Max went to the park with his dad. First, they saw a beautiful kite flying high in the sky. "Let's make one!" said Dad. They worked together and made a colorful kite. When the kite flew up, Max felt completely free and relaxed. At lunchtime, Dad gave Max a big sandwich and some juice. "Today was perfect," Max said. He felt truly happy.
teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• Full W35 mastery: went / saw / felt / made / gave — all five in the park story
• 'felt' used twice again: felt free/relaxed + felt happy — confirms dual use now fully expected
• 'gave' in natural father-child context: Dad GAVE Max lunch — warm, relatable scene
• Culminating drill: 'Tell me about Max's best day in one sentence using 5 verbs.' → 'Max WENT to the park, SAW a kite, MADE a kite with dad, who GAVE him lunch, and he FELT happy.'
• Portfolio: students write 'My Best Day' — must include all 5 W35 verbs

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Project-Based Synthesis
content: Problem: Students have learned over 20 irregular verbs and multiple narrative structures, but often struggle to combine them into a cohesive story.

Solution: This week involves creating an 8-page "Adventure Book." The physical pages force students to break down their narrative into Beginning, Middle (Events + Problem), and End, organically synthesizing all Block B grammar in a fun, personal project.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Draft the Beginning and first Events (Pages 1–3). Focus on movement and perception irregular verbs.
Session 2: Draft the Problem and Solution (Pages 4–6). Focus on accident irregular verbs and feelings.
Session 3: Draft the Ending and Lesson (Pages 7–8). Finalize the book and practice the oral presentation.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Student picks a verb card ("went"), then makes a "Once upon a time" sentence.
S2 pull-out: Show a problem card (e.g., lost key). Student says "I lost my key. I felt worried."
Communicative task (Step 5 - 10 min): Story Exchange. Student A reads their Page 1 and 2. Student B must guess what happens on Page 3.

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W36: went, saw, lost, found, felt
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (went, saw, lost, found, felt) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Review: Past Simple (Irregular & Regular verbs, was/were) + Sequence
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Review: Past Simple (Irregular & Regular verbs, was/were) + Sequence.
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Adventure Stories — Review & Project 3 (My Adventure Book) ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Adventure Stories — Review & Project 3 (My Adventure Book) ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (went, saw, lost, found, felt usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Tells one event from an adventure story using a Past Simple irregular verb (e.g., "I went to the forest and saw a deer").
Student B: Continues the story adding a sequence word (e.g., "Then, I heard a strange sound and felt scared").
Goal: Review saw / heard / felt / went in connected storytelling.

PULL-OUT TASK (S1):
— Ask: "Tell me about a journey — where did you go? What did you see and hear?"
— Scaffold weaker students: "First, I WENT to ___. I SAW ___. I HEARD ___."
— Target elicitation: review ALL irregular forms from Block B — went/came/ran/flew/saw/heard/felt/ate/drank/had.

COMMUNICATIVE TASK TIP:
— Quick fire review: point to a verb card and student gives the Past Simple instantly.
— Stronger students: use 5 different irregular verbs in one connected adventure story.

teacher_contents.reading_passage: Last week, Max went on a forest adventure with his family. First, he saw a beautiful deer drinking from a stream. Then, he heard a strange sound behind a bush. Suddenly, Max saw a huge bear! He ran very fast and hid behind a big rock. His heart felt like it was jumping. "That was so scary!" he said. Finally, they all walked home safely. It was an incredible adventure.
teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• Review week: went / saw / heard / ran / felt — five irregular verbs in a fast-paced adventure
• Also: was/were review — 'he was scared / they were all safe' — connect to earlier blocks
• Sequence words reinforced: First → Then → Suddenly → Finally — all appear naturally in this story
• Error watch: students reverting to present tense in storytelling — all narrative verbs must be Past Simple
• Challenge: students tell the same story using different sequence words (e.g., 'After that' instead of 'Then')

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Starts an adventure story using was/were (e.g., "It was a sunny day. We were at the beach").
Student B: Continues with irregular verbs + sequence words (e.g., "First, we went swimming. Then, we ate ice cream").
Goal: Blend was/were + irregular Past Simple + sequence words.

PULL-OUT TASK (S2):
— Ask: "Describe your BEST day ever — use was/were AND at least 3 irregular verbs."
— Scaffold: "It WAS ___. We WERE at ___. First, we ___. Then, we ___. Finally, we ___."
— Error focus: was vs were — "It WAS sunny. We WERE happy." (not 'we was').

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: fill in the frame — provide WAS/WERE and choose 2 irregular verbs.
— Stronger students: retell a complete adventure with 5+ irregular verbs and all sequence words.

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Science CLIL Integration
content: Problem: Students often know basic vocabulary but struggle to explain scientific concepts using logical reasoning and full sentences.

Solution: We explicitly teach the grammar of reasoning ("because") integrated with the science content (characteristics of life). Students don't just say "It's living"; they must argue "It is living because it breathes and grows."

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce the core characteristics of living things (breathe, grow, move). Focus on basic classification.
Session 2: Practice classifying tricky items (e.g., plants, water, robots). Use "because" and "does not".
Session 3: Full production. Write an explanatory paragraph classifying objects and present the findings orally.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Show a flashcard of an object. The student must classify it and give one reason (e.g., "A rock is non-living because it does not grow.").

Communicative task (Step 5 - 10 min): The Sorting Game. Pairs of students receive a stack of picture cards and must ask each other questions to sort them into "Living" and "Non-Living" piles with spoken reasons.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  What is Living?
content: Detective Luna is investigating: What is living?
Living things are special. They have characteristics.
First, living things BREATHE. Animals breathe air. Fish breathe in water.
Second, living things GROW. A baby grows into an adult. A small plant grows tall.
Third, living things MOVE. Birds fly. Fish swim. Plants move toward the sun.
Living things also NEED food and water to survive.
A cat is a living thing because it breathes, grows, and moves.
A rock is a non-living thing. It is non-living because it does not breathe, grow, or move.
Can you tell if something is living or non-living?
T / F: A rock is a living thing.
T / F: Living things need food and water.

First, he found a little green frog. "The frog is a living thing," Max wrote in his journal. "It is living because it breathes air, moves by jumping, and grows bigger."

After that, Max looked at the river. "Water moves, but is it living?" he thought. "No, water is non-living because it does not breathe or have babies."
Max learned that we must observe carefully to find the truth!

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The Final Science Report
content: Welcome to my final science presentation! I am Detective Luna.

Today I will explain the rules of nature. There are many different things in our world. We divide them into living and non-living things. How do we know the difference? It is easy if you observe carefully!
A living thing is special because it breathes, grows, and moves. It also needs food and water to survive. For example, a cat is a living thing. A tree is a living thing too!
But a plastic chair is a non-living thing. It is non-living because it does not breathe and it does not grow.
You can be a nature detective too! Just look around your house and classify what you see. Science is everywhere!

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Science CLIL Integration
content: Problem: Students know random animal names (dog, snake, frog) but lack the academic vocabulary to classify them logically.

Solution: We explicitly teach 5 scientific classifications (mammal, reptile, amphibian, insect, bird) linked directly to their defining physical traits (hair, scales, smooth skin, six legs, feathers) using the Present Simple tense for universal facts.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce the 5 animal groups and their core physical characteristics. Focus on matching groups to traits.
Session 2: Apply classifications to real-world examples. Practice distinguishing tricky animals.
Session 3: Full production. Write a scientific report classifying multiple animals and present it orally.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Show a picture of an animal (e.g., a snake). Student must classify it and state its defining trait ("It is a reptile. It has scales.").

Communicative task (Step 5 - 10 min): The Animal Sorting Game. Student A has a list of animal traits. Student B has the animal group names. They must ask and answer questions to match them up perfectly.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The Five Animal Groups
content: Detective Max is learning about animal groups in science class.
"We divide living animals into five main groups," says the teacher.
First is the mammal. A mammal is a warm animal that has hair. Dogs and humans are mammals.
Second is the reptile. A reptile is a cold animal that has dry scales. A snake is a reptile.
Third is the amphibian. An amphibian has wet, smooth skin. It can live in water and on land. Frogs are amphibians.
Fourth is the insect. An insect is very small and has exactly six legs. Ants are insects.
Last is the bird. A bird has beautiful feathers and lays eggs.
T / F: A snake is a mammal.
T / F: An insect has six legs.
What does a mammal have on its body?

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  Max Visits the Zoo
content: Yesterday, Detective Max went to the big city zoo to investigate animals.
First, he looked at a big lion. The lion is a mammal because it has warm hair and drinks milk.
Next, he found a cold crocodile sleeping in the sun. The crocodile is a reptile. It has dry, tough scales on its back.
After that, Max saw a wet frog in a small pond. The frog is an amphibian. It has smooth skin and loves to jump.
Then, he watched a tiny ant on a green leaf. The ant is an insect with six legs.
Finally, he saw a colorful parrot. The parrot is a bird with beautiful feathers.
Max loves being a nature detective!

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W38: mammal, reptile, amphibian, insect, bird
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (mammal, reptile, amphibian, insect, bird) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Present Simple for facts (has/have, lays, lives)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Present Simple for facts (has/have, lays, lives).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Nature's Rules — Animal Groups"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Nature's Rules — Animal Groups".

Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (mammal, reptile, amphibian, insect, bird usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

quick_ref.Theme: Nature Detective Academy — The Baby Animal Case

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Science CLIL Integration
content: Problem: Students understand that animals have babies, but they lack the academic terminology and grammatical structures to compare biological processes logically.

Solution: We teach the formal scientific concepts (oviparous vs viviparous) alongside comparative grammar ("unlike", "both", "but"). This empowers students to write and speak like real scientists, moving from simple descriptions to analytical comparisons.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce the core biological concepts of laying eggs (oviparous) vs giving birth (viviparous). Focus on vocabulary and basic contrast ("but").
Session 2: Explore exceptions and tricky animals (platypus, seahorse) to challenge rigid thinking. Practice "Both" and "Unlike".
Session 3: Full production. Write a comprehensive paragraph comparing how different animal groups reproduce and present findings orally.

2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Show a picture of an animal (e.g., a snake). The student must classify its reproduction method ("A snake is oviparous because it lays eggs.").

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  How Do Animals Have Babies?
content: Detective Luna asks: How do animals have babies?
Birds lay eggs in a nest. Baby birds hatch from eggs.
Fish lay eggs in the water.
Reptiles, like snakes and crocodiles, lay eggs on land.
Insects and amphibians lay eggs too!
Second, VIVIPAROUS animals GIVE BIRTH to live babies.
Mammals give birth to babies. Dogs, cats, and humans are mammals.
The babies develop INSIDE the mother before birth.
Baby mammals drink milk from their mother.
The platypus is a mammal, BUT it lays eggs!
Most birds lay eggs. Most mammals give birth.
Which way did YOU come into the world?
T / F: Dogs lay eggs in a nest.
T / F: Oviparous animals lay eggs.
What do baby birds hatch from?
Where do the babies develop before a mammal gives birth?
Fill-in from text: The mother _______________ the baby.
[O] Stage 3B — Inference: Why is the platypus considered a "special case"?

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  Special Animal Babies
content: Yesterday, Max investigated some very special animals.
"Most mammals give birth, but the platypus is different," he read.
"A platypus is a mammal with fur, but it is oviparous. It lays eggs!"
Then, Max learned about the tiny seahorse.
"A seahorse is a fish. Both mother and father protect the babies.
But unlike other fish, the father seahorse carries the eggs. The father gives birth!"
"Many fish lay eggs in the water. But some big sharks are viviparous.
They give birth to live baby sharks. The babies develop inside the mother."
Max was surprised. "Nature is full of secrets!" he said.
"A chicken lays eggs, but a dog gives birth. And some animals break the rules!"
T / F: The platypus gives birth to live babies.
T / F: The father seahorse carries the eggs.
What animal group does the platypus belong to?
Are big sharks oviparous or viviparous?
Fill-in from text: The babies _______________ inside the mother.
[O] Stage 3B — Inference: Why did Max say "Nature is full of secrets"?

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The Animal Museum
content: Welcome to the Animal Museum! I am Detective Luna.
Today, we are learning about how animals have babies.
If you look carefully, you will see two groups.
Over here, we have oviparous animals. They lay eggs.
Both birds and reptiles are in this group. A mother bird builds a nest to protect her eggs. After some time, the eggs hatch.
Over there, we have viviparous animals. They give birth to live babies.
Unlike birds, mammals are viviparous. The babies develop safely inside the mother.
For example, a cat gives birth to cute kittens. The kittens drink milk.
Nature is wonderful because every animal has a special way to grow.
Thank you for visiting the museum today! You are all great science detectives!
T / F: Birds are viviparous animals.
What does a mother bird build to protect her eggs?
Where do the babies of viviparous animals develop?
Fill-in from text: A cat _______________ birth to cute kittens.
[O] Stage 3B — Inference: Why do we say "every animal has a special way to grow"?

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  How Do Animals Have Babies?
content: Detective Luna asks: How do animals have babies?
Birds lay eggs in a nest. Baby birds hatch from eggs.
Fish lay eggs in the water.
Reptiles, like snakes and crocodiles, lay eggs on land.
Insects and amphibians lay eggs too!
Second, VIVIPAROUS animals GIVE BIRTH to live babies.
Mammals give birth to babies. Dogs, cats, and humans are mammals.
The babies develop INSIDE the mother before birth.
Baby mammals drink milk from their mother.
The platypus is a mammal, BUT it lays eggs!
Most birds lay eggs. Most mammals give birth.
Which way did YOU come into the world?

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W39: lay eggs, give birth, hatch, protect, develop
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (lay eggs, give birth, hatch, protect, develop) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Comparison structures (Both, Unlike, but)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Comparison structures (Both, Unlike, but).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Nature's Rules — Oviparous vs Viviparous"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Nature's Rules — Oviparous vs Viviparous".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (lay eggs, give birth, hatch, protect, develop usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Name an animal ("A frog").
Student B: State its reproduction ("A frog lays eggs!").
Goal: Connect animals to their reproduction style.
[O] L3 — Fill in the blank with 3 options (10 items)
A duck _______________ (lays eggs / gives birth / hatches).
A cow _______________ (lays eggs / gives birth / develops).
The small eggs will _______________ (hatch / protect / develop) soon.
The mother bear _______________ (protects / hatches / lays) her cubs.
The baby _______________ (develops / lays / protects) inside the mother.
A snake is _______________ (oviparous / viviparous / mammal).
A cat is _______________ (oviparous / viviparous / bird).
Birds build a _______________ (nest / birth / milk) for their eggs.
Mammals feed their babies _______________ (milk / eggs / nests).
A frog _______________ (lays / gives / hatches) eggs in the water.
[O] L4 — Sentence Expansion (Compare & Contrast) (10 items)
Base: A chicken lays eggs. + Add: (but a dog gives birth) → ________________________________________
Base: A snake is oviparous. + Add: (but a cat is viviparous) → ________________________________________
Base: Birds lay eggs. + Add: (Both / and fish) → ________________________________________

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Emotional Literacy & Expression
content: Problem: Students know basic objects but cannot articulate their emotions or describe regular actions related to emotional well-being.

Solution: Week 4 introduces the "Happy Jar" concept. Students learn to express states of being ("I feel excited/tired") and associate them with positive actions ("I write", "I smile", "I read"). This creates a safe space for emotional expression while practicing the Present Simple tense.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: Pull-out oral tasks (teacher does these with 1–2 students while class works):
S1 pull-out: Show a piece of paper and a jar. Ask: "What do you write?" Student: "I write on the paper."
S2 pull-out: Ask "How do you feel?" Student: "I feel excited."
S3 pull-out: Student reads S3 VC script aloud → teacher notes pronunciation errors → recasts.
Materials needed: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B.
Give Card A to Student A, Card B to Student B.
Students do not show their cards. They ask each other the target question to fill in the missing information.
Students produce complete sentences together to verify answers.

games.materials: Vocab flashcards W4: jar, paper, write, read, smile
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.

instructions: Grammar focus this week: Present Simple (I feel... / I write...) & Emotions.

Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "My World — My Happy Jar"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "My World — My Happy Jar".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (jar, paper, write, read, smile usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

quick_ref.Vocabulary: 6 Tier 1 (production) + 4 Tier 2 (reception)
quick_ref.Theme: Nature Detective Academy — The Habitat Investigation

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Science CLIL Integration
content: Problem: Students often describe places using only basic adjectives (hot, cold, big) without comparing them scientifically.

Solution: We teach the biological concept of habitats alongside comparative grammar (-er than). Students learn to contrast extreme environments (hotter, colder, wetter) and explain why specific animals adapt to each condition.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce the main habitats and basic comparatives. Focus on the mechanics of adding "-er than" to short adjectives.
Session 2: Explore how specific animals adapt to these environments. Practice making complex comparisons between animals and their habitats.
Session 3: Full production. Write a cohesive paragraph comparing two habitats and present it orally to the class.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Show two habitat flashcards (e.g., desert and forest). The student must make a comparative sentence ("The desert is hotter than the forest.").
Communicative task (Step 5 - 10 min): The Habitat Match. Student A describes a habitat's climate using comparatives. Student B must guess the habitat and name an animal that lives there.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  Where Do Animals Live?
content: Every animal has a special home called a habitat (môi trường sống).
Animals live where they can find food, water, and shelter safely.
The desert (sa mạc) is a very hot and dry place. It is hotter (nóng hơn) than the forest!
Camels live in the desert because they can survive without much water.
The rainforest is very wet. It is wetter (ẩm ướt hơn) than the desert.
Monkeys and colorful birds live in the tall rainforest trees.
The polar regions are covered in ice. The Arctic is colder (lạnh hơn) than the ocean (đại dương).
Polar bears live there because they have thick fur to stay warm.
Animals adapt to their habitats to survive!
T / F: The desert is wetter than the rainforest.
T / F: The Arctic is colder than the ocean.
Why do camels live in the desert?
Fill-in from text: The rainforest is _______________ than the desert.
[O] Stage 3B — Inference: Why would a polar bear not survive in the desert?

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W40: habitat, desert, ocean, hotter, colder
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (habitat, desert, ocean, hotter, colder) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Comparatives (-er than)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Comparatives (-er than).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Nature's Rules — Habitats"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Nature's Rules — Habitats".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (habitat, desert, ocean, hotter, colder usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

PART 6: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION — Habitat Changes [ALL]
When Habitats Change
Read this: Animals adapt to their habitats over a long time. But what happens if the habitat changes quickly? If the hot desert becomes colder, the camels might not survive. If the icy polar region gets hotter, the polar bears will lose their ice. We must protect natural habitats!

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Science CLIL Integration
content: Problem: Students know the word "butterfly" or "frog" but cannot scientifically describe how animals grow and change over time.

Solution: We explicitly teach the stages of metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult) integrated with sequence words (First, Next, Then, Finally) and present simple verbs. This allows students to logically describe biological processes step by step.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce the 4 stages of a butterfly's life cycle. Focus on connecting sequence words with the new Tier 1 vocabulary.
Session 2: Explore the life cycle of an amphibian (frog). Compare the stages and practice describing continuous changes in nature.
Session 3: Full production. Write a cohesive scientific report explaining an animal's life cycle from birth to adult, and present it orally.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Show a picture of one life stage (e.g., a pupa). The student must name it and sequence it ("This is the pupa. It is the third stage.").

Communicative task (Step 5 - 10 min): The Cycle Builder. Student A has the pictures out of order. Student B reads the steps using "First, Next...". Student A must arrange the pictures correctly based on the listening.

content: Welcome to my science presentation! I am Detective Max.
Today, I will compare the amazing life cycles of a butterfly and a frog.
Both animals change their bodies a lot.

Next, a larva hatches. The butterfly larva is a hungry worm. The frog larva is a swimming tadpole.

Finally, both animals become adults. The adult butterfly flies in the sky. The adult frog jumps on the land.
Life cycles are wonderful to observe! Thank you for listening!

Every animal has a life cycle (vòng đời). A life cycle has different stages (giai đoạn).

task_cards: S1 Task — "The Cycle Builder"
Materials: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B per pair. Cut along the dotted line.
Instructions for teacher: Give Card A to Student A, Card B to Student B. They must communicate to sequence the life cycle.
Plaintext
🃏 CARD A — Student A | Week 41 S1 — "The Cycle Builder"
Read the butterfly's life cycle out loud to Student B:
1. "First, the butterfly lays an egg."
2. "Next, a hungry larva hatches."
3. "Then, it makes a hard pupa."
4. "Finally, it becomes an adult."
Now, listen to Student B. Write down what happens in stage 2:
🃏 CARD B — Student B | Week 41 S1 — "The Cycle Builder"
Listen to Student A's steps. Write down what happens in stage 3:

1. "First, the frog lays eggs in water."
2. "Next, a tadpole swims out."
3. "Then, it grows legs."
4. "Finally, it is an adult frog."
S2 Task — "The Mystery Stage"
Materials: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B per pair. Cut along the dotted line.
Instructions for teacher: Give Card A to Student A, Card B to Student B. They must describe their mystery stage for the other to guess.

Describe it to Student B: "It hatches from an egg. It is very hungry. It eats leaves. What stage is it?"

Listen to Student A's description.

Describe it to Student A: "It is a hard shell. The insect changes inside safely. It is the third stage. What stage is it?"

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W41: cycle, larva, pupa, adult, stage
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (cycle, larva, pupa, adult, stage) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Sequence Words (First, Next, Then, Finally) + Present Simple
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Sequence Words (First, Next, Then, Finally) + Present Simple.
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "Nature's Rules — Life Cycles"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "Nature's Rules — Life Cycles".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (cycle, larva, pupa, adult, stage usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Science CLIL Integration
content: Problem: Students know words like "rain" or "cloud" but lack the academic vocabulary to explain continuous scientific cycles.

Solution: We explicitly teach the formal scientific terms (evaporation, condensation, precipitation) alongside sequence connectors (First, Then, Next, Finally). This enables students to logically describe a perpetual process using the Present Simple tense.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce the 4 stages of the water cycle. Focus on connecting sequence words with the new Tier 1 academic vocabulary.
Session 2: Explore the journey of a raindrop. Practice describing the continuous changes of water states (liquid to gas to liquid).
Session 3: Full production. Write a cohesive scientific report explaining the entire water cycle, and present it orally to the class.

methodology.title: 2.3 Vocabulary Tiering System
2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: S1 pull-out: Show a picture of one stage (e.g., rain falling). The student must name the academic term ("That is precipitation!").

Communicative task (Step 5 - 10 min): The Cycle Sorter. Student A has the steps out of order. Student B reads the process using "First, Next...". Student A must arrange the flashcards correctly based on the verbal instructions.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT
content: Water goes on an amazing journey! This is called the WATER CYCLE. STEP 1 - EVAPORATION: The sun heats the water in oceans, rivers, and lakes. The water becomes water vapor (gas) and goes UP into the sky. This is called evaporation. STEP 2 - CONDENSATION: The water vapor goes high into the sky. It is cold up there! The water vapor becomes tiny water drops. The drops form clouds. This is called condensation. STEP 3 - PRECIPITATION: The clouds get heavy with water. The water falls down as rain, snow, or hail. This is called precipitation. STEP 4 - COLLECTION: The water collects in oceans and rivers. And the cycle starts again! The water you drink today is very old! It has been cycling for millions of years!
T / F: The water cycle never stops.
T / F: Evaporation makes the water go down into the ground.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT
content: Water goes on an amazing journey! This is called the WATER CYCLE. STEP 1 - EVAPORATION: The sun heats the water in oceans, rivers, and lakes. The water becomes water vapor (gas) and goes UP into the sky. This is called evaporation. STEP 2 - CONDENSATION: The water vapor goes high into the sky. It is cold up there! The water vapor becomes tiny water drops. The drops form clouds. This is called condensation. STEP 3 - PRECIPITATION: The clouds get heavy with water. The water falls down as rain, snow, or hail. This is called precipitation. STEP 4 - COLLECTION: The water collects in oceans and rivers. And the cycle starts again! The water you drink today is very old! It has been cycling for millions of years!
T / F: The water cycle never stops.

Plaintext
🃏 CARD A — Student A | Week 42 S1 — "The Cycle Sorter"
Read the water cycle out loud to Student B:
1. "First, evaporation happens when the sun is hot."
2. "Next, condensation forms white clouds."
3. "Then, precipitation falls as rain."
4. "Finally, the water collects."
Now, listen to Student B. Write down what happens in stage 2:
🃏 CARD B — Student B | Week 42 S1 — "The Cycle Sorter"
Listen to Student A's steps. Write down what happens in stage 3:
Now, read these sentences out loud to Student A:
1. "First, the water becomes invisible vapor."
2. "Next, the vapor cools down in the sky."
3. "Then, the heavy clouds make rain."
4. "Finally, the water flows to the ocean."

S2 Task — "The Mystery Process" Materials: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B per pair. Cut along the dotted line. Instructions for teacher: Give Card A to Student A, Card B to Student B. They must describe their mystery process for the other to guess.
Plaintext

Your mystery process is: EVAPORATION
Describe it to Student B: "The hot sun causes this. Water turns into gas and goes up. What process is it?"
Now listen to Student B's description.

Listen to Student A's description.
Your mystery process is: PRECIPITATION
Describe it to Student A: "This happens when clouds get heavy. Water falls down as rain or snow. What process is it?"

43.unit_theme: The Math Bridge — The "Plus" Machine (Addition Language)

quick_ref.Dual Component:
Math (40m): Addition Language


ELA (80m): Explanatory Writing about Math
quick_ref.Grammar Focus: Present Simple + Sequence Words (First, Next, Then, Finally)
quick_ref.Key Pattern: "First, I add two and three. The sum equals five."
quick_ref.Vocabulary:
Math: add, plus, sum, equals, total


ELA: solve, answer, problem, count, number

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Math CLIL Integration
content: The 80/40 Split: Every 120-minute session is divided into two distinct parts.
Math Component (40 mins): Taught first. Focuses strictly on learning the mathematical vocabulary and reading equations aloud through engaging contexts.
ELA Component (80 mins): Applies the math concepts into writing. Students learn the English skills needed to explain how they solved the math problem step-by-step.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (3 Sessions x 120 Minutes)
content: Session 1: Introduce the basic language of addition (plus, equals, sum) via a story about gathering magical items.
Session 2: Apply addition to real-life word problems (helping an animal). Teach students to identify "clue words" and explain their solving steps logically.
Session 3: Full synthesis. Students write a complete, cohesive explanatory report about working together to solve a practical problem.

vocab_tiers.Memory Trick: S-O-L-V-E: See, Observe, Learn, Verify, Explain

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT (40 Mins)
content: Detective Max is exploring a dark cave. He finds a heavy stone door. There are empty holes in the door.
Suddenly, Max finds 2 glowing blue crystals on the ground. Then, he looks behind a rock and finds 3 shiny red crystals!
To open the door, Max must put all the crystals together. He uses his "Plus Machine" gadget.
The gadget says: "You must ADD the crystals. 2 + 3 = ?"
Max reads the screen: "Two PLUS three EQUALS what?"
He puts them in the holes. Two plus three equals FIVE!
The door opens! The total SUM of the crystals is 5. Adding makes the number bigger!

plus (cộng): Three _______________ (plus / equals) four is seven.
equals (bằng): Four plus one _______________ (equals / adds) five.
sum (tổng): The _______________ (sum / plus) of two and two is four.
total (tổng cộng): Find the _______________ (total / equal) number.

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT (80 Mins)
content: After opening the door, Max writes a letter to Detective Luna to explain his adventure. Detectives must always explain how they solve a mystery!
"Dear Luna, I found a math problem in the cave. Here is how I solved it.
First, I start with the number 2 for the blue crystals.
Next, I add 3 more for the red crystals.
Then, I count all the crystals together in my hand.
Finally, I write the answer in my notebook. The sum equals exactly 5!
Solving puzzles is easy when you explain it step by step!"

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT (40 Mins)
content: Math detectives can help animals solve problems!
Look at this story: "Pip the squirrel is preparing for winter. He has 4 acorns in his tree. Today, he runs to the forest and finds 5 more acorns. How many acorns does Pip have in total?"
Pip is confused, so Detective Luna helps him.
First, she looks for the clue words. The words "more" and "in total" mean we must ADD.
She reads: "Four plus five equals what?"
Let's find the total sum. Four plus five equals NINE. The sum is 9.
Pip is very happy. He has 9 acorns in total to eat this winter!
Word problems are just stories with hidden math!

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT (80 Mins)
content: Today, I will explain how to solve a word problem to help a friend.
The problem is: Luna has 5 red flowers and 4 blue flowers. How many flowers in total?
First, I read the story to find the hidden numbers. The numbers are 5 and 4.
Next, I find the clue word. The word "total" tells me that I must use addition.
Then, I write the math equation on the board: 5 + 4 = 9.
Finally, I write the answer clearly. Five plus four equals nine.
Luna has 9 flowers in total. Following steps makes math easy to explain!

content: Welcome to my final presentation! I am Detective Luna.

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT (40 Mins)
content: Detective Max is exploring a dark cave. He finds a heavy stone door. There are empty holes in the door.
Suddenly, Max finds 2 glowing blue crystals on the ground. Then, he looks behind a rock and finds 3 shiny red crystals!
To open the door, Max must put all the crystals together. He uses his "Plus Machine" gadget.
The gadget says: "You must ADD the crystals. 2 + 3 = ?"
Max reads the screen: "Two PLUS three EQUALS what?"
He puts them in the holes. Two plus three equals FIVE!
The door opens! The total SUM of the crystals is 5. Adding makes the number bigger!

plus (cộng): Three _______________ (plus / equals) four is seven.
equals (bằng): Four plus one _______________ (equals / adds) five.
sum (tổng): The _______________ (sum / plus) of two and two is four.
total (tổng cộng): Find the _______________ (total / equal) number.

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT (80 Mins)
content: After opening the door, Max writes a letter to Detective Luna to explain his adventure. Detectives must always explain how they solve a mystery!
"Dear Luna, I found a math problem in the cave. Here is how I solved it.
First, I start with the number 2 for the blue crystals.
Next, I add 3 more for the red crystals.
Then, I count all the crystals together in my hand.
Finally, I write the answer in my notebook. The sum equals exactly 5!
Solving puzzles is easy when you explain it step by step!"

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT (40 Mins)
content: Math detectives can help animals solve problems!
Look at this story: "Pip the squirrel is preparing for winter. He has 4 acorns in his tree. Today, he runs to the forest and finds 5 more acorns. How many acorns does Pip have in total?"
Pip is confused, so Detective Luna helps him.
First, she looks for the clue words. The words "more" and "in total" mean we must ADD.
She reads: "Four plus five equals what?"
Let's find the total sum. Four plus five equals NINE. The sum is 9.
Pip is very happy. He has 9 acorns in total to eat this winter!
Word problems are just stories with hidden math!

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT (80 Mins)
content: Today, I will explain how to solve a word problem to help a friend.
The problem is: Luna has 5 red flowers and 4 blue flowers. How many flowers in total?
First, I read the story to find the hidden numbers. The numbers are 5 and 4.
Next, I find the clue word. The word "total" tells me that I must use addition.
Then, I write the math equation on the board: 5 + 4 = 9.
Finally, I write the answer clearly. Five plus four equals nine.
Luna has 9 flowers in total. Following steps makes math easy to explain!

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W43: add, plus, sum, equals, solve
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (add, plus, sum, equals, solve) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Present Simple + Sequence Words (First, Next, Then, Finally)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Present Simple + Sequence Words (First, Next, Then, Finally).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "The Math Bridge — The "Plus" Machine (Addition Language)"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "The Math Bridge — The "Plus" Machine (Addition Language)".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (add, plus, sum, equals, solve usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

listening_script.speed_note: Read aloud at a normal, clear pace (85 wpm). Pause 2–3 seconds between sentences. Read the full text twice before students answer questions.
listening_script.text: Welcome to the math lab! Today, we are helping a farmer count his animals. Look at this problem: six plus two equals what? First, I count six brown horses. Then, I add two white horses. I put them in the barn together. The answer is eight! The total sum is eight. Adding makes the total bigger!

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Write an equation on paper (e.g., 5+1=6).
Student B: Read it out loud: "Five plus one equals six. The sum is six."
[O] L3 — Fill in the blank with 3 options (10 items)
Max _______________ (adds / solves / equals) the crystals together.
Two _______________ (plus / sum / total) four equals six.
The answer when you add is the _______________ (sum / add / problem).
Four plus five _______________ (equals / plus / adds) nine.
I will explain how to _______________ (solve / sum / equal) the problem.
_______________ (First / Both), I start with the number six.
_______________ (Next / Finally), I add two more.
When we add, the total gets _______________ (bigger / smaller / colder).
_______________ (Then / First), I count them all together.
_______________ (Finally / Next), I write that the sum is eight.
[O] L4 — Sentence Expansion (Step-by-Step Logic) (10 items)
Base: We add numbers. + Add: (together to make them bigger) → ________________________________________________________________________________
Base: Two plus three. + Add: (equals exactly five) → ________________________________________________________________________________
Base: The sum is five. + Add: (which is the final answer) → ________________________________________________________________________________
Base: I will explain how. + Add: (to solve this math problem) → ________________________________________________________________________________
Base: First, I start with two. + Add: (because I found two blue crystals) → ________________________________________________________________________________
Base: Next, I add three more. + Add: (to the group) → ________________________________________________________________________________
Base: Then, I count them. + Add: (all together carefully) → ________________________________________________________________________________
Base: Finally, I write the answer. + Add: (on my paper) → ________________________________________________________________________________
Base: Math is an important tool. + Add: (for a young detective) → ________________________________________________________________________________
Base: Addition is easy. + Add: (when you follow the steps) → ________________________________________________________________________________
[O] L5 — Paragraph Writing (5 items)
Write a 5-sentence paragraph explaining how to solve this problem: 6 + 3 = 9.
teacher_contents.stem_extension:
STEM/CLIL Extension Notes (teacher only):

PART 5: STEM/CLIL CONNECTION — Visual Math [ALL]
Using Objects to Add
Read this: When we add, we put two groups together to find the total sum. To solve a problem easily, you can use real objects like blocks, apples, or your fingers! If you have 3 blocks and add 2 blocks, you can physically move them and count them all together to find the final answer. Seeing the objects helps our brain learn math faster.
The diagram shows: A math picture showing 3 red apples and a "+" sign, followed by 2 green apples, an "=" sign, and finally a basket with 5 apples inside. The word "SUM" points to the basket.

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Dual Component (Math + ELA)
content: Problem: In Phase 2, students must learn both hard academic concepts (Math) and the language to explain them (ELA), which can cause cognitive overload if taught simultaneously.

Solution: Every session is strictly split. Part 1 (Math Component, 40 mins) focuses purely on the math operation, vocabulary, and logic using engaging detective stories. Part 2 (ELA Component, 80 mins) shifts to the grammatical structures (comparisons, sequencing) needed to explain the math step-by-step.

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT
content: A. Math Reading Input: The Cave of Crystals

Detective Max is exploring a dark cave (hang động). He needs glowing crystals (pha lê) to unlock the magic door. Max finds 10 crystals on the ground. Suddenly, a giant cave bat swoops down! The bat takes away 3 crystals.
"Oh no!" says Max. "This is a subtraction problem. If I have 10 and the bat takes away 3, how many are left?"
He reads it: "Ten minus three equals seven."
He must subtract 3 from 10. The difference is 7. Max has 7 crystals left to unlock the door!
→ Memory trick: M-I-N-U-S: Math Is Not Usually Scary
→ Memory trick: S-U-B: Subtract Unwanted Blocks
→ Memory trick: TAKE: Thieves Always Keep Everything
a. The bat will _______________ away my toy.
b. If you _______________ away two, you have one.
→ Memory trick: L-E-F-T: Look Exactly For Those
→ Key Collocation: how many are left
→ Memory trick: D-I-F-F: Do It Fast Friend

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT
content: A. ELA Reading Input: The Rules of the Cave
To open the door, Max must explain the math rules. He looks at his crystals.
"Addition and subtraction are opposites," Max says. "When we add, the number gets bigger. When we subtract, the number gets smaller."
Max looks at the numbers 10 and 7. "Ten is bigger than seven. Seven is smaller than ten. Because the bat took some away, my final number is smaller."
The magic door hears his perfect English sentences. It slowly opens!

b. Subtraction is the _______________ of addition.

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W44: minus, subtract, take away, left, difference
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (minus, subtract, take away, left, difference) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Comparison structures / Subtraction vs Addition
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Comparison structures / Subtraction vs Addition.

Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Dual Component (Math + ELA)
content: Problem: In Phase 2, students must learn both hard academic concepts (Math/Geometry) and the language to explain them (ELA), which can cause cognitive overload if taught simultaneously.

Solution: Every session is strictly split. Part 1 (Math Component, 40 mins) focuses purely on identifying 2D shapes, sides, and corners using detective logic. Part 2 (ELA Component, 80 mins) shifts to the grammatical structures (descriptive adjectives and contrast words like "but") needed to explain the logic step-by-step.

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT
content: A. Math Reading Input: The City Clues
Max is a great detective. Today, he is studying geometry (hình học). He looks for a clue (manh mối) in the big city.
Max finds a strange, flat shape on the ground.
"Let's count," says Max. "One, two, three, four. It has exactly four equal sides. It also has four sharp corners."
Max knows the answer! "It is a blue square!"
Then, Max finds another shape. He touches it carefully. "This shape has zero straight sides and zero corners. It goes round and round perfectly. It is a bright red circle!"
→ Memory trick: S-H-A-P-E: See How All Patterns End
b. Look at the _______________ on the floor.
→ Memory trick: S-I-D-E: Straight In Different Edges

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT
content: A. Math Reading Input: The City Clues
Max is a great detective. Today, he is studying geometry (hình học). He looks for a clue (manh mối) in the big city.
Max finds a strange, flat shape on the ground.
"Let's count," says Max. "One, two, three, four. It has exactly four equal sides. It also has four sharp corners."
Max knows the answer! "It is a blue square!"
Then, Max finds another shape. He touches it carefully. "This shape has zero straight sides and zero corners. It goes round and round perfectly. It is a bright red circle!"
→ Memory trick: S-H-A-P-E: See How All Patterns End
b. Look at the _______________ on the floor.
→ Memory trick: S-I-D-E: Straight In Different Edges
→ Memory trick: C-O-R: Count Our Right angles
b. Be careful of the sharp _______________.
→ Memory trick: F-L-A-T: Floor Looks Always level Today
b. Put it on the _______________ table.

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT
content: A. ELA Reading Input: Describing the Clues
Max writes descriptive sentences in his notebook to solve the mysterious puzzle.
"First, I found a flat shape. It has four equal sides. Therefore, it is a beautiful square!"
"Next, I found a shape with no straight lines. It has zero corners. Therefore, it is a perfect circle!"
By using adjectives like 'flat', 'equal', and 'sharp', Max can explain the geometry clues clearly to his friends.

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT
content: A. Math Reading Input: Pip Builds a Door
Pip the squirrel needs to build a strong door for his winter house. He finds two new geometry clues in the forest.
First, he finds a green shape. "One, two, three!" Pip counts. "It has exactly three straight sides and three sharp corners. It is a green triangle!"
Next, Pip finds a brown shape. It has four sides like a square, but there is a big difference. Two sides are very long, and two sides are very short.
"Ah!" says Pip. "It is a brown rectangle!"
Triangles and rectangles are perfect for building!
b. The book is a brown _______________.
a. A square has four _______________ sides.

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT
content: A. ELA Reading Input: Describing with "But"
Pip writes a report about his geometry building materials.
"A square has four equal sides. A rectangle has four sides too, but two sides are long and two sides are short!" Pip writes.
The word 'but' helps detectives show a difference.
"The triangle has three straight sides," Pip continues. "It is very strong. I will use the green triangle for my roof, and the brown rectangle for my door."
Pip uses geometry and logic to build the safest house in the forest.
→ Key Collocation: but two sides are
a. It has four sides, _______________ two are long.
b. I like apples, _______________ not bananas.

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W45: shape, side, corner, square, circle
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (shape, side, corner, square, circle) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Adjectives of shape / Descriptive clauses (It has...)
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Adjectives of shape / Descriptive clauses (It has...).
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "The Math Bridge — Detective Max & The Shape Detectives"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "The Math Bridge — Detective Max & The Shape Detectives".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (shape, side, corner, square, circle usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Dual Component (Math + ELA)
content: Problem: In Phase 2, students must learn both hard academic concepts (Math/Logic) and the language to explain them (ELA), which can cause cognitive overload if taught simultaneously.

Solution: Every session is strictly split. Part 1 (Math Component, 40 mins) focuses purely on identifying patterns, rules, and sequences using detective logic. Part 2 (ELA Component, 80 mins) shifts to the grammatical structures ("must be" + sequence words) needed to explain the logic step-by-step.

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT
content: A. Math Reading Input: The Secret Door
Max is a smart detective (thám tử). He finds a secret door. It has a lock (ổ khóa). The lock shows a strange code: Circle, Square, Triangle, Circle, Square...
"There is a missing shape!" says Max. "I must find the rule (quy tắc). It is a repeating pattern (quy luật)."
Max uses his math brain. The shapes repeat in the same order again and again.
"Circle, Square, Triangle," Max says. "If the last shape was a Square, what is next?"
→ Memory trick: P-A-T: Pay Attention Today
b. Look at the _______________ on the door.
→ Memory trick: R-E-P: Read Every Pattern
→ Key Collocation: repeat again and again
→ Memory trick: M-I-S-S: Must Investigate Secret Spaces
→ Memory trick: N-E-X-T: Now Exactly X Times
a. The _______________ shape is a circle.

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT
content: A. ELA Reading Input: Using Logic
Max writes the sequence in his notebook to solve the puzzle (câu đố).
"First, there is a circle. Next, there is a square. Then, there is a triangle. Because the pattern repeats, I can use logic (tư duy logic)!"
Max looks at the lock. "The last shape is a square. Therefore, the next shape must be a triangle!"
When detectives are 100% sure about a pattern, they use the words 'must be'. Max presses the triangle, and the door opens!

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT
content: A. Math Reading Input: Pip's Number Lock
Pip the squirrel has a big wooden box for his winter acorns. The box has a number lock. Pip sees a sequence (chuỗi) of numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8...
"Oh no, I forgot the code!" says Pip. "I must find the missing number to open my box."
Max helps him look at the sequence.
"We must find the rule," says Max. "From 2 to 4, we add 2. From 4 to 6, we add 2. This is a skip-counting pattern!"
Pip smiles. "The rule is add two!"
a. The _______________ is to add two.

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT
content: A. ELA Reading Input: Explaining the Number Sequence
Pip writes down the rule to remember it forever.
"First, the number is two," writes Pip. "Next, the number is four. Then, the number is six. The rule is simple: we always add two."
Max reads the notebook. "So, if the sequence stops at eight, what comes next?"
"Eight plus two is ten," says Pip. "Therefore, the next number must be ten!"
Pip uses his logic to press the number 10. The box opens, and his acorns are safe!
→ Key Collocation: the next number must be
a. The _______________ number must be ten.
→ Key Collocation: pip uses his logic

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT
content: A. Math Reading Input: Pip's Number Lock
Pip the squirrel has a big wooden box for his winter acorns. The box has a number lock. Pip sees a sequence (chuỗi) of numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8...
"Oh no, I forgot the code!" says Pip. "I must find the missing number to open my box."
Max helps him look at the sequence.
"We must find the rule," says Max. "From 2 to 4, we add 2. From 4 to 6, we add 2. This is a skip-counting pattern!"
Pip smiles. "The rule is add two!"
a. The _______________ is to add two.

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT
content: A. ELA Reading Input: Explaining the Number Sequence
Pip writes down the rule to remember it forever.
"First, the number is two," writes Pip. "Next, the number is four. Then, the number is six. The rule is simple: we always add two."
Max reads the notebook. "So, if the sequence stops at eight, what comes next?"
"Eight plus two is ten," says Pip. "Therefore, the next number must be ten!"
Pip uses his logic to press the number 10. The box opens, and his acorns are safe!
→ Key Collocation: the next number must be
a. The _______________ number must be ten.
→ Key Collocation: pip uses his logic

games.name: Vocab Slam
games.session_fit: All formats — best after vocab intro (P3) in any session
games.materials: Vocab flashcards W46: pattern, rule, next, missing, repeat
instructions: Round 1: Teacher calls a Vietnamese meaning — first student to say the English word AND use it correctly in a sentence wins the card.
Round 2: Reverse — teacher calls English word, student gives Vietnamese + memory trick.
Bonus round: Students chain all vocab words (pattern, rule, next, missing, repeat) into one connected story using sequence connectors from this week.
Team variant: 2 teams, 10 cards per round. Team with highest score wins.

games.name: Grammar Relay
games.session_fit: Best in Drill slot (Slot 2) or after P4/P6 in 3-session mode
games.materials: 10 sentence cards — 5 correct, 5 with errors based on: Modals of Deduction (must be) + Sequence Words
instructions: Grammar focus this week: Modals of Deduction (must be) + Sequence Words.
Speed Read: Display sentence for 5 sec. Teams write C (correct) or E (error) on whiteboards simultaneously — no copying allowed.
Fix-It: For error sentences, team that corrects fastest AND explains the rule earns double points.
Build: Each team member adds 1 original sentence using the grammar target. The chain must be logically connected — each sentence must link to the previous.

games.name: Story Race
games.session_fit: All formats — best in final slot of the week (S3 / Slot 5 / Session B)
games.materials: Story starter card: theme "The Math Bridge — Detective Max & The Pattern Code"
instructions: Give each pair a story starter connected to this week's theme: "The Math Bridge — Detective Max & The Pattern Code".
Pair A adds 2 sentences — must include at least 2 vocab words from this week.
Pass to Pair B: they MUST correct any grammar mistake from Pair A first, then add 2 more sentences using different vocab words.
Final round: Each pair presents their story ending aloud. Class votes on most creative + most accurate (pattern, rule, next, missing, repeat usage). Teacher scores grammar precision.

methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Dual Component (Math + ELA)
content: Problem: In Phase 2, students must learn both hard academic concepts (Math/Place Value) and the language to explain them (ELA), which can cause cognitive overload if taught simultaneously.

Solution: Every session is strictly split. Part 1 (Math Component, 40 mins) focuses purely on reading big numbers, counting zeroes, and understanding digit positions. Part 2 (ELA Component, 80 mins) shifts to the grammatical structures needed to articulate these numbers clearly in English sentences.

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT
content: A. Math Reading Input: The Bank Vault
Detective Max finds a secret bank vault (hầm chứa). It is a huge metal door. Max needs to find the code.
"The password (mật khẩu) is a big number," says Max. "I must understand the digits (chữ số)."
Max looks at his notes. "The number 100 is one hundred. It has three digits. One, zero, and another zero."
Max thinks. "If I add one more zero, the number gets bigger! The number 1,000 is one thousand. It has exactly four digits."
By counting the digits and the zeroes, Max can crack the code!
→ Memory trick: H-U-N: Has Usually Noughts
→ Memory trick: T-H-O: Three Huge zeroes

→ Memory trick: D-I-G: Dig Into Geometry
→ Memory trick: Z-E-R-O: Zeros Equal Round Objects

"Next, I look at the number one thousand. It has exactly four digits. Because one thousand has more digits, it is a bigger number!"
Max presses 1, 0, 0, 0 on the keypad. The heavy metal door slowly opens. Understanding how to describe big numbers makes math very easy!
