parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  A research report is a structured piece of academic writing that presents findings from research. It is different from a story (narrative) because it focuses on facts, evidence, and analysis rather than a sequence of events.
content: 📖 A research report is a structured piece of academic writing that presents findings from research. It is different from a story (narrative) because it focuses on facts, evidence, and analysis rather than a sequence of events.

The structure of a research report has three main parts. The INTRODUCTION tells the reader what the report is about, why the topic is important, and what the report will cover. A good introduction has a 'hook' — an interesting fact or question — followed by background information, and finally a thesis statement: your answer to the Main Research Question.

The BODY contains multiple paragraphs, each focusing on one sub-question. Each body paragraph uses the PEEL structure: Point (main idea), Evidence (quote or paraphrase), Explanation (what the evidence means), Link (connect to the next paragraph or restate the point).
The CONCLUSION summarizes the key findings and restates the answer to the Main Question in new words.

listening_script.text:
A powerful introduction has THREE essential elements. First, the HOOK: one or two sentences that immediately grab attention. The best hooks use a surprising statistic, a thought-provoking question, or a vivid description. Second, BACKGROUND: 2-3 sentences giving context. What is the topic? Why is it important? Third, the THESIS STATEMENT: a clear, confident statement of your main argument or finding. The thesis tells the reader exactly what the report will prove or show.
There are four common hook types: Statistical hook ('1 million tonnes of plastic enter the ocean every day.'), Question hook ('What if all ocean fish disappeared by 2050?'), Fact hook ('The blue whale is the largest animal ever to exist on Earth.'), Scenario hook ('Imagine a world where water is more expensive than gold.').

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  A report is more than a collection of paragraphs — it is an argument that FLOWS. Each paragraph should connect smoothly to the next, so the reader is guided through your thinking step by step.
content: 📖 A report is more than a collection of paragraphs — it is an argument that FLOWS. Each paragraph should connect smoothly to the next, so the reader is guided through your thinking step by step.

TRANSITIONS are the bridges between paragraphs. A weak report just jumps from one idea to the next. A strong report uses transitions to show relationships: How does this paragraph add to the previous one? Does it contrast? Does it give an example? Does it move from problem to solution?

There are several types of transitions: Adding transitions ('Furthermore...', 'In addition...', 'Moreover...') show you are expanding on an idea. Contrasting transitions ('However...', 'On the other hand...', 'In contrast...') show a different perspective. Cause-effect transitions ('As a result...', 'Therefore...', 'Consequently...') connect cause and effect. Concluding transitions ('To summarize...', 'Overall...', 'In conclusion...') signal the end.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  The conclusion is your final opportunity to make an impression on your reader. A weak conclusion just repeats the introduction word-for-word. A powerful conclusion does three things: it SUMMARIZES, it RESTATES, and it CALLS TO ACTION.
content: 📖 The conclusion is your final opportunity to make an impression on your reader. A weak conclusion just repeats the introduction word-for-word. A powerful conclusion does three things: it SUMMARIZES, it RESTATES, and it CALLS TO ACTION.
First, SUMMARIZE the key findings from your body paragraphs. Briefly remind the reader of the most important evidence you presented. Use different words from your body paragraphs — do not copy.
Second, RESTATE your thesis. This is your main argument, expressed in new language. It should feel like the logical endpoint of all your evidence.

Third, END WITH IMPACT. This might be a CALL TO ACTION ('Therefore, governments and individuals must...'), a FINAL THOUGHT ('Ultimately, our actions today will determine...'), or a QUESTION TO THE READER ('What will you do to help solve this problem?').
A conclusion should NEVER introduce new ideas or new evidence. Everything in the conclusion should come from what you already discussed.

First, SUMMARIZE the key findings from your body paragraphs. Briefly remind the reader of the most important evidence you presented. Use different words from your body paragraphs — do not copy.
Second, RESTATE your thesis. This is your main argument, expressed in new language. It should feel like the logical endpoint of all your evidence.
Third, END WITH IMPACT. This might be a CALL TO ACTION ('Therefore, governments and individuals must...'), a FINAL THOUGHT ('Ultimately, our actions today will determine...'), or a QUESTION TO THE READER ('What will you do to help solve this problem?').
A conclusion should NEVER introduce new ideas or new evidence. Everything in the conclusion should come from what you already discussed.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  Proofreading is the FINAL step before submitting any written work. It focuses on ACCURACY — catching grammar errors, spelling mistakes, punctuation problems, and formatting issues.
content: 📖 Proofreading is the FINAL step before submitting any written work. It focuses on ACCURACY — catching grammar errors, spelling mistakes, punctuation problems, and formatting issues.

Professional proofreaders use specific techniques: Read ALOUD — your ear catches errors your eye misses. Read BACKWARDS (sentence by sentence from the end) — this forces you to focus on each sentence individually. Use a CHECKLIST — systematically check one type of error at a time. CHECK CITATIONS — are all sources cited? Are citation formats consistent?

Common errors in student writing include: subject-verb agreement ('The data show' not 'The data shows'), tense consistency (stick to present tense for facts), apostrophes (it's = it is; its = belonging to it), comma splices (two sentences joined with only a comma — use a full stop or a connecting word).
After proofreading, your report is ready for its FINAL FORMAT — title page, headings, bibliography.

listening_script.text:
Professional proofreaders use specific techniques: Read ALOUD — your ear catches errors your eye misses. Read BACKWARDS (sentence by sentence from the end) — this forces you to focus on each sentence individually. Use a CHECKLIST — systematically check one type of error at a time. CHECK CITATIONS — are all sources cited? Are citation formats consistent?
Common errors in student writing include: subject-verb agreement ('The data show' not 'The data shows'), tense consistency (stick to present tense for facts), apostrophes (it's = it is; its = belonging to it), comma splices (two sentences joined with only a comma — use a full stop or a connecting word).
After proofreading, your report is ready for its FINAL FORMAT — title page, headings, bibliography.
dictation: Use a CHECKLIST — systematically check one type of error at a time.
CHECK CITATIONS — are all sources cited?

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  A great oral presentation has three qualities: CLARITY (the audience can understand you), CONFIDENCE (you believe in your content), and CONNECTION (you engage with your audience).
content: 📖 A great oral presentation has three qualities: CLARITY (the audience can understand you), CONFIDENCE (you believe in your content), and CONNECTION (you engage with your audience).

The structure of a 10-minute research presentation follows these sections: OPENING (1-2 min) — greet the audience, introduce yourself and your topic, give a hook. OVERVIEW (30 sec) — tell the audience what you will cover: 'Today I will present...'. BODY (5-6 min) — present your key findings, one sub-question at a time, using your visual aids. DATA SECTION (1 min) — explain your chart or graph. CONCLUSION (1 min) — summarize findings and state your thesis answer. Q&A (2 min) — answer questions from the audience.

The most important presentation skills are: SIGNPOSTING (telling the audience where you are in the presentation), maintaining EYE CONTACT (look at the audience, not your notes), speaking at an appropriate PACE (not too fast), and using GESTURES to emphasize key points.
(↑ Re-read the story above to answer:)

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  Rehearsal is the key to a confident presentation. Professional speakers rehearse 5-10 times before presenting. Each rehearsal improves fluency, timing, and confidence.
content: 📖 Rehearsal is the key to a confident presentation. Professional speakers rehearse 5-10 times before presenting. Each rehearsal improves fluency, timing, and confidence.
The FIRST rehearsal is the most uncomfortable — that is normal! You will stumble over words, forget what comes next, and speak too fast or too slow. This is exactly what rehearsal is for.

During rehearsal, practice these skills: PACING — speak slowly and clearly. A common mistake is rushing when you are nervous. PAUSING — a 2-3 second pause between sections sounds professional and helps the audience process information. EYE CONTACT — look up from your notes every 2-3 sentences. VOLUME — speak loudly enough for everyone in the room to hear.
After your rehearsal, your peer evaluator will give you feedback using a structured rubric. This feedback is a GIFT — it shows you exactly what to work on before the real presentation.

listening_script.text:
The FIRST rehearsal is the most uncomfortable — that is normal! You will stumble over words, forget what comes next, and speak too fast or too slow. This is exactly what rehearsal is for.
During rehearsal, practice these skills: PACING — speak slowly and clearly. A common mistake is rushing when you are nervous. PAUSING — a 2-3 second pause between sections sounds professional and helps the audience process information. EYE CONTACT — look up from your notes every 2-3 sentences. VOLUME — speak loudly enough for everyone in the room to hear.
After your rehearsal, your peer evaluator will give you feedback using a structured rubric. This feedback is a GIFT — it shows you exactly what to work on before the real presentation.

listening_script.text:
What is Argumentative Writing?
Argumentative writing tries to CONVINCE the reader to agree with your OPINION.
KEY ELEMENTS:
1. CLAIM (Thesis)
- Your main argument
- What you believe and will prove
- Example: "Homework should be banned in primary schools."
2. REASONS
- WHY you believe your claim
- At least 3 strong reasons
- Example: "Homework causes stress."
3. EVIDENCE
- FACTS that support your reasons
- Statistics, examples, expert opinions
- Example: "Studies show 70% of students feel stressed about homework."
4. COUNTERARGUMENT
- The OTHER SIDE's argument
- Show you understand different views
- Example: "Some people say homework helps students practice."
5. REBUTTAL
- Why the other side is wrong
- Example: "However, students can practice in class instead."
Good argumentative writing is LOGICAL, ORGANIZED, and PERSUASIVE!
dictation: Argumentative writing tries to CONVINCE the reader to agree with your OPINION.

listening_script.text:
Good arguments need EVIDENCE - facts that prove your point.
TYPES OF EVIDENCE:
1. STATISTICS (Numbers)
- "70% of students report feeling stressed about homework."
- "Students spend an average of 3 hours on homework daily."
2. EXPERT OPINIONS
- "Dr. Smith, a child psychologist, says homework is harmful."
- "The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends limited homework."
3. EXAMPLES
- "In Finland, students have almost no homework and perform well."
- "My neighbor's child became sick from homework stress."
4. RESEARCH STUDIES
- "A Stanford study found homework causes physical health problems."
- "Research shows homework has little benefit for young children."
5. LOGICAL REASONING
- "If students spend 6 hours at school plus 3 hours on homework,
they have only 3 hours for play, which is not healthy."
STRONG EVIDENCE is:
- From reliable sources
- Relevant to your argument
- Specific (not vague)
dictation: Good arguments need EVIDENCE - facts that prove your point.

listening_script.text:
A COUNTERARGUMENT is the OTHER SIDE's view.
A REBUTTAL is your response - why they're wrong.
INCLUDING COUNTERARGUMENTS MAKES YOUR ESSAY STRONGER because:
1. Shows you understand different views
2. Makes you seem fair and logical
3. Lets you prove why your side is better
HOW TO WRITE A COUNTERARGUMENT:
Step 1: State the opposing view
"Some people argue that homework is necessary for practice."
Step 2: Acknowledge any valid points
"It is true that practice is important for learning."
Step 3: REBUT - explain why your view is better
"However, students can practice during school hours instead.
After-school time should be for rest and play."
PHRASES FOR COUNTERARGUMENTS:
- Some people believe...
- Opponents argue that...
- It is often said that...
- Critics claim that...
PHRASES FOR REBUTTALS:
- However, this argument is flawed because...
- Nevertheless, research shows...
- Despite this claim, the evidence suggests...
- While this may seem true, actually...
dictation: A COUNTERARGUMENT is the OTHER SIDE's view.
A REBUTTAL is your response - why they're wrong.

INCLUDING COUNTERARGUMENTS MAKES YOUR ESSAY STRONGER because:
1.

To write a strong argumentative essay, you must understand BOTH sides of the debate. Today, we research the strongest arguments IN FAVOR of children having smartphones.

ARGUMENT 2 — EDUCATION & LEARNING: Educational apps, online libraries, and learning platforms expand learning beyond school. Research shows children with supervised internet access score higher in reading.
ARGUMENT 3 — DIGITAL LITERACY: In a digital world, early exposure to technology prepares children for modern society. Students who learn responsible tech use early develop better self-regulation.

listening_script.text:
The classic argumentative essay has 5 paragraphs: Introduction (thesis), Body 1 (strongest argument), Body 2 (second argument), Body 3 (counterargument + refutation), Conclusion.
Notice that Paragraph 3 is a COUNTERARGUMENT PARAGRAPH. This is the advanced move that separates a good essay from a great one.
STRUCTURE OF COUNTERARGUMENT PARAGRAPH:
Sentence 1 (CONCEDE): 'Admittedly, / It is true that / Proponents of [opposite view] argue that [strongest opposing point].'
Sentence 2 (EVIDENCE FOR OPPOSITION): 'They support this claim with [evidence for opposing side].'
Sentence 3 (TRANSITION): 'However, / Nevertheless, / Despite this,'
Sentence 4 (REFUTATION): '[Your strongest counter-evidence].'
Sentence 5 (CONCLUSION OF REFUTATION): 'Therefore, while [opposing view] has some merit, [your position] is ultimately more supported by the evidence.'
dictation: Notice that Paragraph 3 is a COUNTERARGUMENT PARAGRAPH.
This is the advanced move that separates a good essay from a great one.

parts.title: PART 1: READING INPUT  FORMAL DEBATE STRUCTURE
content: A formal Oxford-style debate has two teams: AFFIRMATIVE (FOR the motion) and NEGATIVE (AGAINST). Each team has a First Speaker, a Second Speaker, and a Rebuttal Speaker.
• Motion announced: 'This house believes that children under 12 should NOT be allowed smartphones.'
• Affirmative 1st Speaker (2 min): Defines terms + presents Team's main argument
• Negative 1st Speaker (2 min): Rejects affirmative argument + presents Team's main argument
• Affirmative 2nd Speaker (2 min): Presents second affirmative argument
• Negative 2nd Speaker (2 min): Presents second negative argument
• Affirmative Rebuttal (1 min): Responds to ALL negative arguments
• Floor Questions (5 min): Audience asks questions to either team
